Negative queryset slicing raises in Django; comment's safety claim is false

When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise `ValueError` ("Negative indexing is not supported"). Any admin-supplied cursor with a negative offset, e.g. `?cursor=0:-5:0`, therefore produces a 500.

The comments state the ORM "properly handles negative slicing automatically" and that this "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds". Both are wrong, and the second describes an intent to bypass pagination bounds that should not ship. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError`, as the other paginators do.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: passing a negative `cursor.offset` as `start_offset` to queryset slicing when `enable_advanced_features` is True.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Comment claims negative offset support but no code changed

The new comment says negative offsets are allowed for "efficient reverse pagination". `Cursor` was already doing a plain `int(offset)`, and no behaviour changed.

The similar comment added in `BasePaginator.get_result` (paginator.py line 179) is also misleading. A negative offset with `is_prev` is still passed straight to the queryset slice, which raises in Django.

These comments misdocument the pagination contract and should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same underlying bug: in BasePaginator.get_result, when cursor.is_prev is True, a negative offset is passed directly to the queryset slice without clamping, which causes an error.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes on the datetime key it is used with

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on `getattr(item, self.key)`. The audit log endpoint uses it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so the value is a `datetime`. `build_cursor` calls the key function on the first result, which raises `TypeError` and returns a 500 for any non-empty page.

`value_from_cursor` (line 843) has a related problem. It returns the raw integer cursor value, and `build_queryset` then emits `datetime <= <int>`, which Postgres rejects.

The optimized path is therefore unusable. It needs the `DateTimePaginator` key/cursor conversion, e.g. by subclassing `DateTimePaginator`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on a `datetime` value (from `order_by='-datetime'`), resulting in a `TypeError`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AttributeError on default path when organization_context.member is None

`enable_advanced` is computed unconditionally, even when `optimized_pagination` was not requested, and dereferences `organization_context.member.has_global_access`. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` for callers that are not org members, such as staff sessions and API-key/token authenticated requests.

For these callers `request.user.is_superuser` is False, so the expression raises `AttributeError` and the endpoint returns 500. This is a regression to the existing, non-optimized audit log listing. Only evaluate this when `use_optimized` is true, and guard for `member is None`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: accessing `organization_context.member.has_global_access` will raise an `AttributeError` when the user is neither a superuser nor an organization member (causing `organization_context.member` to be `None`).

false_positives.candidate:
Privilege gate uses raw is_superuser flag instead of active superuser session

The gate uses `request.user.is_superuser`, which is true for any account with the superuser flag. It does not check whether the superuser session is active (sudo/elevated). Sentry's convention is `is_active_superuser(request)`.

As written, a flagged user with no active superuser session who has org access gets the "admin-only" pagination behaviour.

Spans are silently evicted with no metric or log

Before this change, oversized segments were detected at flush time and reported via the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric plus `logger.error`. That check was removed from `_load_segment_data`.

The new `zpopmin` eviction in the Lua script drops the lowest-scored spans whenever a segment exceeds 1000. Nothing is returned to the caller and nothing is emitted, so span data is lost with no observability.

The script should return the evicted count so Python can emit a metric, or the old metric should be kept in some form.

max_segment_spans config is now dead; limit hardcoded in Lua with a different value

`SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001), but nothing reads it anymore. The actual cap is the literal `1000` hardcoded in `add-buffer.lua`.

Callers that tune `max_segment_spans` will see no effect, and the default disagrees with the enforced value. Pass the limit to the script as an ARGV, or remove the parameter.

ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregate, corrupting scores on duplicate payloads

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the parent_key merge on line 53) uses the default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same payload is present in both sets, its score becomes the sum of two timestamps (~3.4e9), for example after a Kafka redelivery of a span.

That inflated score makes the duplicate effectively unevictable and breaks the end-timestamp ordering that `zpopmin` relies on. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or `MIN`) to keep scores meaningful.

Evicted spans leave stale entries in the redirect hash

`zpopmin` removes payloads from the segment set, but their `span_id -> set_span_id` entries in `span-buf:sr:{...}` are never removed. `done_flush_segments` only `hdel`s the span IDs of spans actually flushed.

Since the redirect hash's TTL is refreshed on every insert for the trace, these entries linger. Late children of an evicted span can also be redirected into an already-flushed segment key.

Redirect depth limit silently reduced 10x and explanatory comment removed

The redirect-following loop limit was cut from 10000 to 1000. The comment explaining that trees deeper than the limit may not be joined correctly was also deleted.

This behaviour change is unrelated to eviction and is not mentioned in the PR. Segment trees deeper than 1000 levels will now be split into separate segments.

No tests for span eviction or the new optimized audit-log pagination

The tests were only updated to pass `end_timestamp_precise`. Nothing exercises the new core behaviour: inserting more than 1000 spans into a segment and asserting which spans are evicted (lowest end timestamp), including across merges via `zunionstore`.

Likewise there are no tests for `OptimizedCursorPaginator` or the `optimized_pagination=true` audit log path. Even a basic test would have caught that the path crashes on its datetime key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses outer `dataset` and `request.GET['query']` instead of the per-call dataset and query

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` and `query`, but the eligibility check is called with the closed-over outer `dataset` and `request`. `_is_error_focused_query` then reads `request.GET['query']` rather than the query actually being executed.

In the dashboard split path, `_get_event_stats(discover, ..., f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction")` and the ERROR_EVENTS split both run against discover. However, the decision is made against the outer metrics dataset, which always returns False, so error counts there are never upsampled.

Conversely, the upsampling verdict for any call reflects the user's original query string, not the modified split query. Results for the same widget can therefore differ depending on which code path served them.

Pass `scoped_dataset` and the effective `query` to the eligibility check.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`, causing it to skip upsampling in the dashboard split path where the outer dataset is metrics and the scoped dataset is discover. It also notes the related issue with the query string.

false_positives.candidate:
Substring check treats negated `!event.type:error` queries as error-focused

`_is_error_focused_query` lowercases the raw query string and checks whether it contains `"event.type:error"`. That substring also appears in the negation `!event.type:error`, in `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, and in free text such as `message:"event.type:error"`.

For these discover-dataset queries in allowlisted projects, `count()` is rewritten to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` even though the matched rows are not (or not only) errors. Transactions and other non-error rows have no meaningful `sample_weight`, so the chart silently shows wrong counts, typically 0 or undercounted.

The check should parse the query (e.g. with the event search parser) and require a positive `event.type:error` filter, not a substring match.

"Performance" cache adds a remote cache round-trip to every events-stats call, even for non-error datasets

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` does `cache.get` (and `cache.set` on a miss) before checking the dataset. Every `_get_event_stats` call therefore hits the shared cache backend (memcached/redis), including spans, transactions, metrics, logs and RPC queries that can never be upsampled.

Dashboard split requests call `_get_event_stats` up to four times, so they pay several round-trips.

The value being cached is a single `options.get` lookup, which Sentry's options manager already serves from an in-process cache. The "optimization" replaces a local lookup with a network call and writes one cache key per distinct project-id combination.

Check `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` first and drop the extra cache layer, or at minimum short-circuit before touching the cache.

Allowlist changes are served stale for 60s and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is unusable/never called

Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds per (org, project-set). The docstring says `invalidate_upsampling_cache` "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes", but nothing calls it.

It also cannot be called meaningfully. The allowlist is a single global option, and the cache is keyed on arbitrary combinations of project ids. An options change has no way to enumerate which keys to delete.

As a result, removing a project from the allowlist (e.g. because upsampled data is wrong) keeps producing upsampled counts for up to a minute across all workers. Adding one keeps returning raw counts for the same period. Mixed results within a dashboard are possible.

The key also embeds `hash(tuple(...))`, which can in principle collide between different project sets. Either remove the cache or key and invalidate it on the option value itself.

`options.get(key, [])` passes `[]` as `silent`, not as a default; real option path is never tested

`OptionsManager.get(key, silent=False)` has no default-value parameter. The `[]` is interpreted as `silent=[]` and is not used as a fallback value.

If `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is not registered in this codebase, `options.get` raises `UnknownOption`. Because the helper is now called on every events-stats request, that would turn every request into a 500.

All new tests patch the whole `options` module, so the real lookup is never exercised. Drop the misleading second argument, ensure the option is registered, and add a test that does not mock `options`.

Top-events ranking uses raw `count()` while the plotted series are upsampled

For top events, only `timeseries_columns` are transformed. `selected_columns=self.get_field_list(...)`, `orderby=self.get_orderby(...)` and `equations` still use plain `count()`.

The top-N groups are therefore chosen and ordered by raw (sampled) counts, while the plotted values are upsampled. Groups with different client sample rates can display in an order that contradicts their plotted values, and equations referencing `count()` mix raw and upsampled numbers.

`upsampled_count` is exposed as a public function and changes the `count` result type to `number`

Unlike the neighbouring internal helpers, the new `SnQLFunction("upsampled_count", ...)` is not marked `private=True`. Any user can call `upsampled_count()` directly in discover or errors queries, including against data where `sample_weight` is not populated. That makes an internal implementation detail part of the public query API.

It also declares `default_result_type="number"`, while `count()` is `integer`. The response meta for the `count` column now changes type for allowlisted projects, which affects frontend formatting and any API consumer relying on the type.

Accidental gitlink/submodule `sentry-repo` committed

The PR adds `sentry-repo` as a subproject commit pointing at the base commit, with no `.gitmodules` entry. This is clearly an accidental artifact of a local checkout. It adds a broken submodule to the repository root, which can confuse clones, CI checkouts and tooling. It should be removed from the PR.

Docstrings/comments contradict actual caching behavior

The `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` docstring says it "reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time… intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state". Its only caller caches the result for 60s, so this is false.

In the endpoint, "This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution" and "late transformation ensures we use the most current schema assumptions" also describe nothing the code actually does. The decision is recomputed per `_get_event_stats` call, and `upsampling_enabled = should_upsample` is a no-op alias.

The transform branches inside the `use_rpc` paths are dead code, because `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` always returns False for `spans_rpc`/`ourlogs`. These comments will mislead future maintainers.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every not-allowed Check now triggers a full permission DB query

Previously a cached permission map answered both allows and denials. Now any Check whose cached scopes don't grant access falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which always runs `permissionStore.GetUserPermissions` against the DB. The denial cache is keyed per (name, folder), so it only protects repeat checks of the same resource.

A user with restricted access who triggers checks over many distinct resources pays one permission query per unseen denied resource. This happens with search results filtered item by item, or batch checks over hundreds of dashboards. Singleflight only dedupes concurrent identical calls.

This is a significant DB load amplification compared to before.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same change in code behavior: cached permission grants are trusted immediately, while denials from the cached permission map are ignored and fall through to a fresh DB query (`getIdentityPermissions`). However, they focus on completely opposite implications—the golden comment flags the security risk of trusting stale cached grants, whereas the candidate flags the performance risk (DB load amplification) of not trusting cached denials. Because they identify the exact same underlying code logic and asymmetric caching mechanism, there is a partial/semantic overlap in the code issue identified, though the framed problem (security vs performance) differs.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test seeds a non-granting permission, so it passes without the denial cache

The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the seeded map is `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. `checkPermission` treats a false value as no access.

Without the denial cache, the flow would still end in a deny. The cached perms don't allow access, the fallback DB query on the default fakeStore returns no permissions, and the result is `Allowed: false`. The test therefore passes regardless of whether the denial cache works.

The value should be `true` so that only the denial entry explains the deny. There is also no test that a DB-confirmed denial actually writes a denial entry.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug in the test: the comment says it's seeding permissions to 'allow access', but the map actually sets `dashboards:uid:dash1` to `false`, which means `checkPermission` treats it as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ambiguous '_' separator in denial key causes collisions between different resources

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins name and parent folder with `_`. Grafana dashboard and folder UIDs may themselves contain underscores, so distinct (name, parent) pairs map to the same key. For example, dashboard `abc` in folder `def_ghi` and dashboard `abc_def` in folder `ghi` both produce `..._abc_def_ghi`.

A denial on one resource then wrongly denies the other for the cache TTL.

The key also reuses the `.perm_` prefix of `userPermCacheKey` in the same underlying cache, which makes the key spaces harder to reason about.

Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or encode or length-prefix the components, and use a distinct prefix such as `.perm_denial_`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses underscores to join components, which can cause key collisions if the components themselves contain underscores, leading to incorrect permission denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous denials also deny the renderer

The denial key is built from `checkReq.UserUID`, the raw id parsed from the subject, and does not include `checkReq.IdentityType`. Different identity types can share that id. Anonymous (`anonymous:0`) and the render service (`render:0`) both parse to UserUID "0".

If an anonymous user is denied `dashboards:read` on dashboard X, the entry `<ns>.perm_0_dashboards:read_X_<folder>` is cached. A renderer check for X within the next 30s then hits that entry and is denied, even though `getRendererPermissions` would grant `*`. This breaks alert screenshots and reports. The reverse also applies: renderer denials leak to anonymous checks.

Include the identity type in the key, or the resolved internal user UID for users and service accounts.

Denial cache is consulted before the fresh DB re-query, re-introducing stale denials

The PR's goal is to let a user access a resource as soon as the permission exists, by re-querying the DB when cached permissions don't allow access. However, the denial cache is checked first and short-circuits that re-query for the full 30s TTL.

Any denial recorded for a (user, action, name, folder) tuple keeps the user locked out after the permission is granted. Examples:
- an existence probe or GET on a UID before the dashboard was created;
- a check that raced with the default creator permissions being written;
- an admin granting access right after a 403.

The new 'requery on miss' path never runs in those cases. Consider not caching denials for resources that may be newly created, using a much shorter TTL, or invalidating denial entries when permissions are refetched.

Disabling the client-side cache in-proc makes every Check deserialize full cached permission maps

With `NoopCache` on the in-proc client, every access check goes through the in-proc gRPC server. Each one performs several cache `Get`s, and each `Get` JSON-unmarshals its value: the denial entry, the user identifiers, and the full scope map for the action, which can contain thousands of entries for large instances.

Previously the authlib client cached per-check results. For hot paths such as batch or item checks this adds noticeable CPU and allocation overhead per request.

Meanwhile the remote/cloud client (line 162) still caches results, including denials, for 30s, so the newly-created-resource problem this PR targets remains in cloud mode.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is a static, predictable value (pipeline.signature)

`pipeline.signature` is an md5 of the pipeline view class names. It is the same for every user, org and session; the tests hard-code `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` across different users and orgs. Using it as the OAuth `state` gives no CSRF or code-injection protection: anyone can compute it, so a forged callback `?code=<attacker code>&state=<constant>` passes the check at line 412.

The PR description presents state validation as a security property, but it doesn't provide one. Generate a random nonce (for example `secrets.token_hex()`), store it in pipeline state, and compare it with `constant_time_compare`, as `OAuth2LoginView`/`OAuth2CallbackView` already do.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same security vulnerability as the golden comment: using the static `pipeline.signature` as the OAuth `state` parameter instead of generating a random nonce per request.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when existing Integration metadata has no `sender`

The new check reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with no fallback. `sender` is only written when the Integration is created by the installation webhook (`state.get("sender")` in `build_integration`). Integrations created through the pipeline itself never get it; `test_basic_flow` asserts the metadata has no `sender` key. Integrations created before sender tracking also lack it.

Common case: an org uninstalls the GitHub integration in Sentry. The OrganizationIntegration is deleted but the Integration row stays. On reinstall, the code reaches this branch and raises an unhandled KeyError, so the user gets a 500 and cannot reinstall.

The lookup is also not filtered by `provider`, so a non-GitHub integration with a colliding `external_id` would fail the same way. Use `.get()` with a defined fallback (verify another way, or error cleanly), and filter by `provider="github"`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: accessing `integration.metadata['sender']['login']` without checking if the `'sender'` key exists, which raises a `KeyError` when `sender` metadata wasn't set during creation.

false_positives.candidate:
User/installation ownership check skipped when no Integration row exists

If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises DoesNotExist, the view goes straight to `pipeline.next_step()` without comparing `github_authenticated_user` to anything. `build_integration` then fetches the installation using the app JWT, which can read any installation of the app. It links the installation to the current Sentry org.

The attack this PR targets (supplying someone else's installation_id) therefore still works whenever no Integration row exists yet. Examples:
- the window before the installation webhook is processed;
- failed or delayed webhook deliveries;
- self-hosted instances that don't receive GitHub webhooks.

GitHub installation IDs are sequential and easy to enumerate. A stronger check is to use the OAuth token from `OAuthLoginView` to confirm the installation appears in the user's `GET /user/installations`, and do that in every branch.

Network/HTTP failures in token exchange or user lookup cause unhandled 500s

`safe_urlopen(...)` on line 423 sits outside the try block, so connection errors or timeouts propagate. `get_user_info()` calls `raise_for_status()` internally, so a 401 or 5xx from `api.github.com/user` (for example a revoked token or a GitHub outage) raises an uncaught HTTPError. In both cases the user sees a 500 instead of the integration-failed dialog. That dialog is what the opener window expects for its postMessage. Wrap these calls and return `error(...)` on failure.

test_installation_not_found no longer tests the not-found path

The test now sends a deliberately wrong `state` (`ddd023...`). The new state-mismatch check rejects it before the GitHub 404 is ever reached, and the assertion was changed to `"Invalid installation request."`.

It then passes `{ ...request, targets }` (with `filters` intact) to `runSplitQuery`. That function now calls `applyTemplateVariables` again on every sub-request. `runQuery` → `super.query` applies it a third time.

For queries with a parser or label filters, each ad hoc filter is appended three times to the expression sent to Loki. Variable values are also re-templated twice. The updated test asserting `applyTemplateVariables` was called 5 times (1 + 4 sub-requests) codifies this redundant re-interpolation instead of catching it. Interpolation should happen once, e.g. by clearing `filters` on the request handed to `runSplitQuery`, or by having `runSplitQuery` skip interpolation when called from the shard path.

It then asserts that the expression sent to `runQuery` is `count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])`. The real `LokiDatasource.applyTemplateVariables` deliberately strips `__auto` (and `__range*`, `__interval*`) from scopedVars so these are interpolated on the backend. In production `$__auto` stays as-is.

The test therefore documents behaviour that doesn't exist. The same pattern is copied into `shardQuerySplitting.test.ts` (around line 88). Neither test covers the realistic case: a dashboard variable in `step` affecting `calculateStep` grouping, or ad hoc filters combined with splitting. As a result they would not catch the duplicated-filter regression.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback chain depends on per-site default_locale but the translation LRU cache ignores it

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds the fallback chain from `SiteSetting.default_locale`, which differs per site in multisite and can be changed by an admin at runtime. The process-wide LRU cache in `I18n.translate` (translate_accelerator.rb, `k = "#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`) is keyed only by key, requested locale and backend.

Scenario: a user on site A (default `de`) requests a key that is missing in `ja`. The `de` fallback string is cached. A `ja` user on site B (default `fr`) in the same process then gets site A's German text. The same staleness happens after an admin changes `default_locale`: earlier fallback results stay cached until the process restarts.

- Sidekiq jobs and mailers
- rake tasks
- controllers or middleware outside ApplicationController
- `I18n.t(..., locale: x)` calls

In those paths a key missing from the current locale falls back to locales whose translations were never loaded, so the lookup returns "translation missing: ...". For argument-less `I18n.t` calls that string is frozen into the shared LRU cache under `key+locale`. Fix: load the fallback chain inside the patched `I18n.translate` / `load_locale`, not in a controller filter.

The PR adds a custom fallback order (user locale → site default → en), changes the loading path (`ensure_loaded!`), and turns fallbacks on in every environment, including test and development. No tests cover any of it.

There is no check that:
- a key missing in the user locale resolves from the site default locale, then from English;
- the fallback locales get loaded;
- cached translations behave correctly when the default locale changes.

Regressions such as the cache and loading issues in this change would go unnoticed.

When the feed content later changes, `PostRevisor.new(nil).revise!` raises NoMethodError. `PollFeed` loops over all items without rescue, so one deleted embed aborts processing of every later feed item on every hourly run. The throttle calls `setnx` and then `expire` in a separate command. If the process dies or Redis errors between the two calls, the key never expires and that embed URL is treated as 'retrieved recently' forever. Use a single atomic `SET key 1 NX EX 60`.

When feed polling is enabled, each cache miss calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline. That downloads the whole feed and runs `TopicEmbed.import` for every item. Together with the per-URL throttle (bypassable via distinct URLs), requests for unknown URLs can repeatedly trigger full feed downloads and imports.

The `--category` option was removed, so existing invocations that pass `-c` will fail. Topics are no longer created with the thread's original `created_at`. `feed_polling_enabled` defaults to false and is not stubbed to true in the 'requires feed_polling_url' and 'requires embed_by_username' examples. `poll_feed` is therefore never called no matter what the URL or username checks do, so these tests do not verify the conditions they describe. `embeddable_host` is blank by default, so `ensure_embeddable` raises InvalidAccess (403) before `params.require(:embed_url)` runs. The example only asserts `should_not be_success`, so it passes without exercising the missing-parameter path its name describes. There is also no coverage for a referer whose host doesn't match.

This PR changes an existing migration to `create_table :top_topics, force: true`. Editing a released migration has no effect where it has already run. Where it hasn't, it now silently drops any existing `top_topics` table. The new `create_topic_embeds` migration uses `force: true` the same way. The change is unrelated to embedding and should be reverted.

`t.string :embed_url` creates a varchar(255) column. Article URLs with long slugs or query strings can exceed this, and PostgreSQL then raises 'value too long' during `TopicEmbed.create!`. That fails the import job, or aborts the feed loop. Use `text`, or validate/truncate the length.

On any day with a date override, the user's existing Cal bookings and connected-calendar busy times are therefore ignored. `getWorkingHours` splits ranges that cross UTC midnight into two entries with shifted `days`. Example: a PST user working Mon–Fri 9–17 gets {days 1–5, 1020–1439} and {days 2–6, 0–60}.

- A Tuesday 00:30Z slot is rejected by the first entry.

- Slots during the organizer's day D (e.g. D 17:00Z = 09:00 PST) don't match, so normal working hours apply and they are wrongly offered.

Tokens from these grants are therefore encoded with the unknown grant `na`, even though shortcuts `cc` and `pg` were added to their factories. This silently defeats the feature for the client-credentials case. No test catches it, because `expectClientLogin` does not check `TOKEN_ID`.

`getShortcut()` is added to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` without a default implementation.

Any custom `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` compiled against the previous SPI will throw `AbstractMethodError` when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` calls `gtf.getShortcut()`, which prevents server startup. A custom implementation returning `null` would instead cause an NPE from `ConcurrentHashMap.put`.

Consider a default implementation (or a fallback to `na`) and handling of null shortcuts instead of failing boot.

Public copy constructor Context(Context) removed from SPI class

The public `OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context)` copy constructor is deleted rather than updated to copy the new `grantType` field.

Custom grant implementations or wrappers that used it to derive or modify a context will fail to compile or link. This removal is unrelated to the feature, which only needed the new field copied. Keep the constructor and copy `grantType` in it.

Lazy map refresh can silently overwrite existing shortcut mappings

`postInit` detects duplicate shortcuts by comparing map sizes. The lazy refresh in `getShortcutByGrantType` and `getGrantTypeByShortcut` instead blindly `put`s into both maps.

A newly deployed grant whose shortcut collides with an existing one would overwrite the mapping in `grantsByShortcuts`. Previously issued tokens would then decode to the wrong grant type, and the two maps would become inconsistent. The two maps are also updated non-atomically.

The refresh paths should apply the same collision and length validation, e.g. via `putIfAbsent` and rejecting conflicts.

The access token `jti` changes from a 36-char UUID to a prefixed form, e.g. `onrtac:<uuid>`, 43 chars containing `:`.

Resource servers or integrations that parse or validate `jti` as a UUID, or store it in fixed-length/UUID-typed columns for replay detection, will break after upgrade. This externally visible format change is not documented in upgrade/migration notes in this PR.

- `testWrongVersions` only checks the error text, not that the exit code is now 3.

On any partition revocation, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the current strategy. That calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets every worker's `shutdown` flag, calls `Queue.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the workers.

On the next assignment, arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` again and the new strategy wraps the same dead pool. Each `submit` then goes through `FixedQueuePool.submit`: `add_offset` succeeds, but `work_queue.put` raises `queue.ShutDown`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches that exception and marks the offset completed, so the commit thread commits it.

Result: after the first rebalance (deploy, scale event, pod restart), no uptime result is processed, yet all offsets are committed. This is silent data loss.

The shared `OffsetTracker` makes it worse. Stale outstanding or committable offsets for revoked partitions survive into the new assignment. They can block commits forever, or be passed to arroyo's `stage_offsets` for unassigned partitions; that raises, and the whole commit batch fails every tick.

Fix: the pool and tracker should be owned per strategy, or reset on assignment. `close()` should not tear down a resource owned by the factory.

Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which ends up in arroyo's `StreamProcessor` commit callback. That callback calls `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets`/`commit_offsets` and updates the commit-policy state. Arroyo expects it to be called only from the processing thread, inside `submit`/`poll`/`join`. Here it runs concurrently with the main thread's `consumer.poll()` and with rebalance callbacks, with no synchronization.

Consequences:
- Races on arroyo's unsynchronized internal state (staged offsets, policy timestamps).
- Exceptions when staging offsets for partitions that were just revoked.
- Commits with `force=False` under `ONCE_PER_SECOND` may only be staged. Because the loop calls commit only when new offsets become committable, the trailing offsets can sit staged indefinitely once traffic pauses.

The committable offsets should be computed and committed from `poll()` on the main thread, as arroyo's `CommitOffsets` step does. `join()` should do a final forced commit.

Unbounded queues mean no backpressure, despite the docstring's claim

Each worker queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`. `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`, so arroyo never pauses the consumer. If processing is slower than ingestion (slow DB or cache, one hot queue), the consumer keeps reading the topic into memory. Every message, with its full `Message` object, is held in `WorkItem`, and the `OffsetTracker` sets grow alongside.

This can OOM the consumer. Because commits stay behind the slowest item, a crash also forces reprocessing of a very large backlog.

The class docstring (line 253) promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which is not true. Bound the queues, and raise `MessageRejected` from `submit` when the target queue is full.

join() ignores its timeout, shutdown blocks up to 5s per worker, and no final commit is made

`join(timeout)` discards the timeout and calls `close()`. `close()` waits up to 5s for the commit thread. It then calls `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`, which calls `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` on each worker in turn. With the default of 20 queues and workers stuck in slow processing, a rebalance or shutdown can block for about 100s, regardless of arroyo's `join_timeout`. That risks exceeding `max.poll.interval.ms` and triggering further rebalances.

`terminate()`, which is meant to be immediate, also goes through the same blocking `pool.shutdown()`.

In addition, the commit thread is stopped before the workers finish, and no final commit is issued. Offsets completed since the last 1s tick are never committed and will be reprocessed after every rebalance.

Honor the timeout, shut workers down in parallel, and force-commit completed offsets in `join()`.

Offset-gap tests assert behaviour the tracker only exhibits for one commit tick

`test_offset_gaps_block_commits` (and `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` in the uptime tests) assert that a missing offset 101 prevents committing past 100.

The tracker does not keep blocking. After committing 100, `mark_committed` prunes `all_offsets` to {102, 103}. On the next tick, `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` jumps to 102, and the tracker commits 103 without 101 ever arriving.

The unit test only reaches 103 on its second wait because of this, not because 101 was submitted. The uptime test passes only because it stops observing before the second 1s tick.

These tests give false confidence about the gap semantics and are timing-dependent. Either change the semantics or make the tests assert what the code actually guarantees.

Queue-depth gauge emitted for every message, and worker gauges overwrite each other

Every processed item emits `metrics.gauge("remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth", ...)` in the worker's `finally` block. On a high-volume topic like uptime results, that is one statsd call per message per worker.

The gauge is tagged only with `identifier`, not with the worker or queue id. The values reported by different workers therefore overwrite each other, and the metric does not show any particular queue's depth.

`poll()` already reports total queue depth; per-queue depth could be emitted there, tagged by queue index.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.

Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise `ValueError` ("Negative indexing is not supported"). Any admin-supplied cursor with a negative offset, e.g. `?cursor=0:-5:0`, therefore produces a 500.

The comments state the ORM "properly handles negative slicing automatically" and that this "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds". Both are wrong, and the second describes an intent to bypass pagination bounds that should not ship. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError`, as the other paginators do.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The new comment says negative offsets are allowed for "efficient reverse pagination". `Cursor` was already doing a plain `int(offset)`, and no behaviour changed.

This matches the golden issue of failing to clamp the offset, despite the candidate framing it as misleading documentation.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on `getattr(item, self.key)`. `value_from_cursor` (line 843) has a related problem. It returns the raw integer cursor value, and `build_queryset` then emits `datetime <= <int>`, which Postgres rejects.

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AttributeError on default path when organization_context.member is None

`enable_advanced` is computed unconditionally, even when `optimized_pagination` was not requested, and dereferences `organization_context.member.has_global_access`. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` for callers that are not org members, such as staff sessions and API-key/token authenticated requests.

For these callers `request.user.is_superuser` is False, so the expression raises `AttributeError` and the endpoint returns 500. This is a regression to the existing, non-optimized audit log listing. Only evaluate this when `use_optimized` is true, and guard for `member is None`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify an unguarded organization_context.member.has_global_access dereference that raises AttributeError for non-superuser, non-member callers. Although they describe a different nullable component of the access chain, they point to the same underlying missing-null-guard issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Privilege gate uses raw is_superuser flag instead of active superuser session

The gate uses `request.user.is_superuser`, which is true for any account with the superuser flag. It does not check whether the superuser session is active (sudo/elevated). Sentry's convention is `is_active_superuser(request)`.

As written, a flagged user with no active superuser session who has org access gets the "admin-only" pagination behaviour.

Spans are silently evicted with no metric or log

Before this change, oversized segments were detected at flush time and reported via the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric plus `logger.error`. That check was removed from `_load_segment_data`.

The new `zpopmin` eviction in the Lua script drops the lowest-scored spans whenever a segment exceeds 1000. Nothing is returned to the caller and nothing is emitted, so span data is lost with no observability.

The script should return the evicted count so Python can emit a metric, or the old metric should be kept in some form.

max_segment_spans config is now dead; limit hardcoded in Lua with a different value

`SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001), but nothing reads it anymore. The actual cap is the literal `1000` hardcoded in `add-buffer.lua`.

Callers that tune `max_segment_spans` will see no effect, and the default disagrees with the enforced value. Pass the limit to the script as an ARGV, or remove the parameter.

ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregate, corrupting scores on duplicate payloads

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the parent_key merge on line 53) uses the default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same payload is present in both sets, its score becomes the sum of two timestamps (~3.4e9), for example after a Kafka redelivery of a span.

That inflated score makes the duplicate effectively unevictable and breaks the end-timestamp ordering that `zpopmin` relies on. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or `MIN`) to keep scores meaningful.

Evicted spans leave stale entries in the redirect hash

`zpopmin` removes payloads from the segment set, but their `span_id -> set_span_id` entries in `span-buf:sr:{...}` are never removed. `done_flush_segments` only `hdel`s the span IDs of spans actually flushed.

Since the redirect hash's TTL is refreshed on every insert for the trace, these entries linger. Late children of an evicted span can also be redirected into an already-flushed segment key.

Redirect depth limit silently reduced 10x and explanatory comment removed

The redirect-following loop limit was cut from 10000 to 1000. The comment explaining that trees deeper than the limit may not be joined correctly was also deleted.

This behaviour change is unrelated to eviction and is not mentioned in the PR. Segment trees deeper than 1000 levels will now be split into separate segments.

No tests for span eviction or the new optimized audit-log pagination

The tests were only updated to pass `end_timestamp_precise`. Nothing exercises the new core behaviour: inserting more than 1000 spans into a segment and asserting which spans are evicted (lowest end timestamp), including across merges via `zunionstore`.

Likewise there are no tests for `OptimizedCursorPaginator` or the `optimized_pagination=true` audit log path. Even a basic test would have caught that the path crashes on its datetime key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses outer `dataset` and `request.GET['query']` instead of the per-call dataset and query

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` and `query`, but the eligibility check is called with the closed-over outer `dataset` and `request`. `_is_error_focused_query` then reads `request.GET['query']` rather than the query actually being executed.

In the dashboard split path, `_get_event_stats(discover, ..., f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction")` and the ERROR_EVENTS split both run against discover. However, the decision is made against the outer metrics dataset, which always returns False, so error counts there are never upsampled.

Conversely, the upsampling verdict for any call reflects the user's original query string, not the modified split query. Results for the same widget can therefore differ depending on which code path served them.

Pass `scoped_dataset` and the effective `query` to the eligibility check.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer dataset rather than scoped_dataset, causing discover-backed dashboard split queries to skip upsampling when the original dataset is metrics. Its additional concern about the effective query does not negate this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Substring check treats negated `!event.type:error` queries as error-focused

`_is_error_focused_query` lowercases the raw query string and checks whether it contains `"event.type:error"`. That substring also appears in the negation `!event.type:error`, in `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, and in free text such as `message:"event.type:error"`.

For these discover-dataset queries in allowlisted projects, `count()` is rewritten to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` even though the matched rows are not (or not only) errors. Transactions and other non-error rows have no meaningful `sample_weight`, so the chart silently shows wrong counts, typically 0 or undercounted.

The check should parse the query (e.g. with the event search parser) and require a positive `event.type:error` filter, not a substring match.

"Performance" cache adds a remote cache round-trip to every events-stats call, even for non-error datasets

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` does `cache.get` (and `cache.set` on a miss) before checking the dataset. Every `_get_event_stats` call therefore hits the shared cache backend (memcached/redis), including spans, transactions, metrics, logs and RPC queries that can never be upsampled.

Dashboard split requests call `_get_event_stats` up to four times, so they pay several round-trips.

The value being cached is a single `options.get` lookup, which Sentry's options manager already serves from an in-process cache. The "optimization" replaces a local lookup with a network call and writes one cache key per distinct project-id combination.

Check `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` first and drop the extra cache layer, or at minimum short-circuit before touching the cache.

Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds per (org, project-set). The docstring says `invalidate_upsampling_cache` "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes", but nothing calls it.

It also cannot be called meaningfully. The allowlist is a single global option, and the cache is keyed on arbitrary combinations of project ids. An options change has no way to enumerate which keys to delete.

As a result, removing a project from the allowlist (e.g. because upsampled data is wrong) keeps producing upsampled counts for up to a minute across all workers. Adding one keeps returning raw counts for the same period. Mixed results within a dashboard are possible.

The key also embeds `hash(tuple(...))`, which can in principle collide between different project sets. Either remove the cache or key and invalidate it on the option value itself.

`options.get(key, [])` passes `[]` as `silent`, not as a default; real option path is never tested

`OptionsManager.get(key, silent=False)` has no default-value parameter. The `[]` is interpreted as `silent=[]` and is not used as a fallback value.

If `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is not registered in this codebase, `options.get` raises `UnknownOption`. Because the helper is now called on every events-stats request, that would turn every request into a 500.

All new tests patch the whole `options` module, so the real lookup is never exercised. Drop the misleading second argument, ensure the option is registered, and add a test that does not mock `options`.

For top events, only `timeseries_columns` are transformed. `selected_columns=self.get_field_list(...)`, `orderby=self.get_orderby(...)` and `equations` still use plain `count()`.

The top-N groups are therefore chosen and ordered by raw (sampled) counts, while the plotted values are upsampled. Groups with different client sample rates can display in an order that contradicts their plotted values, and equations referencing `count()` mix raw and upsampled numbers.

`upsampled_count` is exposed as a public function and changes the `count` result type to `number`

Unlike the neighbouring internal helpers, the new `SnQLFunction("upsampled_count", ...)` is not marked `private=True`. Any user can call `upsampled_count()` directly in discover or errors queries, including against data where `sample_weight` is not populated. That makes an internal implementation detail part of the public query API.

It also declares `default_result_type="number"`, while `count()` is `integer`. The response meta for the `count` column now changes type for allowlisted projects, which affects frontend formatting and any API consumer relying on the type.

Accidental gitlink/submodule `sentry-repo` committed

The PR adds `sentry-repo` as a subproject commit pointing at the base commit, with no `.gitmodules` entry. This is clearly an accidental artifact of a local checkout. It adds a broken submodule to the repository root, which can confuse clones, CI checkouts and tooling. It should be removed from the PR.

The `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` docstring says it "reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time… intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state". Its only caller caches the result for 60s, so this is false.

In the endpoint, "This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution" and "late transformation ensures we use the most current schema assumptions" also describe nothing the code actually does. The decision is recomputed per `_get_event_stats` call, and `upsampling_enabled = should_upsample` is a no-op alias.

The transform branches inside the `use_rpc` paths are dead code, because `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` always returns False for `spans_rpc`/`ourlogs`. These comments will mislead future maintainers.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every not-allowed Check now triggers a full permission DB query

Previously a cached permission map answered both allows and denials. Now any Check whose cached scopes don't grant access falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which always runs `permissionStore.GetUserPermissions` against the DB. The denial cache is keyed per (name, folder), so it only protects repeat checks of the same resource.

A user with restricted access who triggers checks over many distinct resources pays one permission query per unseen denied resource. This happens with search results filtered item by item, or batch checks over hundreds of dashboards. Singleflight only dedupes concurrent identical calls.

This is a significant DB load amplification compared to before.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same asymmetric permission-cache behavior: cached grants are accepted, while cached denials fall through to a database lookup. It emphasizes DB load rather than the golden comment's stale-grant security risk, but points to the same underlying code issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test seeds a non-granting permission, so it passes without the denial cache

The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the seeded map is `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. `checkPermission` treats a false value as no access.

Without the denial cache, the flow would still end in a deny. The cached perms don't allow access, the fallback DB query on the default fakeStore returns no permissions, and the result is `Allowed: false`. The test therefore passes regardless of whether the denial cache works.

The value should be `true` so that only the denial entry explains the deny. There is also no test that a DB-confirmed denial actually writes a denial entry.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same mismatch: the test claims cached permissions allow dashboard access, but the seeded permission is false, so checkPermission still denies access. Its additional observations do not change this core match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ambiguous '_' separator in denial key causes collisions between different resources

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins name and parent folder with `_`. Grafana dashboard and folder UIDs may themselves contain underscores, so distinct (name, parent) pairs map to the same key. For example, dashboard `abc` in folder `def_ghi` and dashboard `abc_def` in folder `ghi` both produce `..._abc_def_ghi`.

A denial on one resource then wrongly denies the other for the cache TTL.

The key also reuses the `.perm_` prefix of `userPermCacheKey` in the same underlying cache, which makes the key spaces harder to reason about.

Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or encode or length-prefix the components, and use a distinct prefix such as `.perm_denial_`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underscore-delimited cache key ambiguity and collision risk in userPermDenialCacheKey, including an example of distinct resource components producing identical keys and causing incorrect denial cache hits. The additional prefix concern does not change this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous denials also deny the renderer

The denial key is built from `checkReq.UserUID`, the raw id parsed from the subject, and does not include `checkReq.IdentityType`. Different identity types can share that id. Anonymous (`anonymous:0`) and the render service (`render:0`) both parse to UserUID "0".

If an anonymous user is denied `dashboards:read` on dashboard X, the entry `<ns>.perm_0_dashboards:read_X_<folder>` is cached. A renderer check for X within the next 30s then hits that entry and is denied, even though `getRendererPermissions` would grant `*`. This breaks alert screenshots and reports. The reverse also applies: renderer denials leak to anonymous checks.

Include the identity type in the key, or the resolved internal user UID for users and service accounts.

Denial cache is consulted before the fresh DB re-query, re-introducing stale denials

The PR's goal is to let a user access a resource as soon as the permission exists, by re-querying the DB when cached permissions don't allow access. However, the denial cache is checked first and short-circuits that re-query for the full 30s TTL.

Any denial recorded for a (user, action, name, folder) tuple keeps the user locked out after the permission is granted. Examples:
- an existence probe or GET on a UID before the dashboard was created;
- a check that raced with the default creator permissions being written;
- an admin granting access right after a 403.

The new 'requery on miss' path never runs in those cases. Consider not caching denials for resources that may be newly created, using a much shorter TTL, or invalidating denial entries when permissions are refetched.

Disabling the client-side cache in-proc makes every Check deserialize full cached permission maps

With `NoopCache` on the in-proc client, every access check goes through the in-proc gRPC server. Each one performs several cache `Get`s, and each `Get` JSON-unmarshals its value: the denial entry, the user identifiers, and the full scope map for the action, which can contain thousands of entries for large instances.

Previously the authlib client cached per-check results. For hot paths such as batch or item checks this adds noticeable CPU and allocation overhead per request.

Meanwhile the remote/cloud client (line 162) still caches results, including denials, for 30s, so the newly-created-resource problem this PR targets remains in cloud mode.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is a static, predictable value (pipeline.signature)

`pipeline.signature` is an md5 of the pipeline view class names. It is the same for every user, org and session; the tests hard-code `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` across different users and orgs. Using it as the OAuth `state` gives no CSRF or code-injection protection: anyone can compute it, so a forged callback `?code=<attacker code>&state=<constant>` passes the check at line 412.

The PR description presents state validation as a security property, but it doesn't provide one. Generate a random nonce (for example `secrets.token_hex()`), store it in pipeline state, and compare it with `constant_time_compare`, as `OAuth2LoginView`/`OAuth2CallbackView` already do.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: OAuth state uses the static pipeline.signature instead of a fresh per-request random value, undermining state-based CSRF protection.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when existing Integration metadata has no `sender`

The new check reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with no fallback. `sender` is only written when the Integration is created by the installation webhook (`state.get("sender")` in `build_integration`). Integrations created through the pipeline itself never get it; `test_basic_flow` asserts the metadata has no `sender` key. Integrations created before sender tracking also lack it.

Common case: an org uninstalls the GitHub integration in Sentry. The OrganizationIntegration is deleted but the Integration row stays. On reinstall, the code reaches this branch and raises an unhandled KeyError, so the user gets a 500 and cannot reinstall.

The lookup is also not filtered by `provider`, so a non-GitHub integration with a colliding `external_id` would fail the same way. Use `.get()` with a defined fallback (verify another way, or error cleanly), and filter by `provider="github"`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unchecked access to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"], which raises a KeyError when sender metadata was not set during integration creation. Its additional observations do not change this core match.

false_positives.candidate:
User/installation ownership check skipped when no Integration row exists

If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises DoesNotExist, the view goes straight to `pipeline.next_step()` without comparing `github_authenticated_user` to anything. `build_integration` then fetches the installation using the app JWT, which can read any installation of the app. It links the installation to the current Sentry org.

The attack this PR targets (supplying someone else's installation_id) therefore still works whenever no Integration row exists yet. Examples:
- the window before the installation webhook is processed;
- failed or delayed webhook deliveries;
- self-hosted instances that don't receive GitHub webhooks.

GitHub installation IDs are sequential and easy to enumerate. A stronger check is to use the OAuth token from `OAuthLoginView` to confirm the installation appears in the user's `GET /user/installations`, and do that in every branch.

Network/HTTP failures in token exchange or user lookup cause unhandled 500s

`safe_urlopen(...)` on line 423 sits outside the try block, so connection errors or timeouts propagate. `get_user_info()` calls `raise_for_status()` internally, so a 401 or 5xx from `api.github.com/user` (for example a revoked token or a GitHub outage) raises an uncaught HTTPError. In both cases the user sees a 500 instead of the integration-failed dialog. That dialog is what the opener window expects for its postMessage. Wrap these calls and return `error(...)` on failure.

test_installation_not_found no longer tests the not-found path

The test now sends a deliberately wrong `state` (`ddd023...`). The new state-mismatch check rejects it before the GitHub 404 is ever reached, and the assertion was changed to `"Invalid installation request."`.

As a result, the `build_integration` 404 path (`"The GitHub installation could not be found."`) is untested. The test name is also misleading. Use the correct state so the flow reaches the 404, and add a separate test for state mismatch.

There is also no test where an Integration exists with a matching `sender` and the install succeeds, and none where `sender` is missing (the KeyError case).

The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper{updated: obj}`, so legacy received exactly the object that unified storage persisted.

The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update`. Legacy therefore calls `objInfo.UpdatedObject` against its own (possibly stale) old object. Preconditions and resourceVersion carried from the client may also not match legacy's state.

This causes silent divergence between the stores, which mode 3 writes to legacy precisely to avoid. Pass `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}` instead.

- legacy is written asynchronously after a successful storage write;
- legacy is not written when storage fails;

For queries with a parser or label filters, each ad hoc filter is appended three times to the expression sent to Loki. Variable values are also re-templated twice. The updated test asserting `applyTemplateVariables` was called 5 times (1 + 4 sub-requests) codifies this redundant re-interpolation instead of catching it. Interpolation should happen once, e.g. by clearing `filters` on the request handed to `runSplitQuery`, or by having `runSplitQuery` skip interpolation when called from the shard path.

It then asserts that the expression sent to `runQuery` is `count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])`. The real `LokiDatasource.applyTemplateVariables` deliberately strips `__auto` (and `__range*`, `__interval*`) from scopedVars so these are interpolated on the backend. In production `$__auto` stays as-is.

The test therefore documents behaviour that doesn't exist. The same pattern is copied into `shardQuerySplitting.test.ts` (around line 88). Neither test covers the realistic case: a dashboard variable in `step` affecting `calculateStep` grouping, or ad hoc filters combined with splitting. As a result they would not catch the duplicated-filter regression.

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` in one session and the INSERT/upsert in a separate session, with no transaction or locking. When the count is just under the limit, several concurrent requests from new devices (on one instance or across HA instances) can all see `count < deviceLimit` and all insert. The limit can therefore be exceeded by the level of concurrency. If it is meant as a hard cap, the check and insert need to be atomic, e.g. a conditional INSERT ... SELECT with the count in the WHERE clause, or a transaction with appropriate locking.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same check-then-insert race: concurrent requests can pass the device count check and insert devices beyond the limit without atomicity or locking.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. Only the first request from a new device over the limit is rejected. For the next ~29 minutes (cache TTL), `localCache.Get(key)` hits, `tagDeviceUI` returns nil, and `Anonymous.Authenticate` lets the device in. The device is never stored or counted, so a user who just reloads the page is admitted. The cache entry should only be set after a successful create/update, or removed on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice and retains it on ErrDeviceLimitReached, causing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the 29-minute cache expiration.

Enforcement depends on `TagDevice` returning `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. `TagDevice` returns nil early when the client-controlled `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is missing (and also when the remote address can't be parsed). In both cases `Anonymous.Authenticate` succeeds. Any client that does not send the header (curl, scripts, a modified frontend) gets anonymous access regardless of the configured limit, and is never counted. If the limit is meant to be enforced, requests without a device ID should be handled explicitly once the limit is reached.

Device tagging moved into the request path unconditionally, even when no limit is set

The goroutine with its own timeout and panic recovery was replaced by a synchronous `TagDevice(ctx, ...)` call for every deployment, including the default `device_limit = 0`. Every anonymous request that misses the local cache now waits for a DB upsert before authentication completes. With a limit set, it also waits for an extra `COUNT(*)` over `anon_device`. The panic recovery was also dropped. Consider keeping the asynchronous path when `AnonymousDeviceLimit == 0` and only blocking when enforcement is needed.

DI wiring for AnonStore likely broken by the ProvideAnonDBStore signature change

`ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` used to receive `anonstore.AnonStore` via dependency injection, so a provider for it (`anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` plus a bind) was registered in the wire set. `ProvideAnonDBStore` now requires an `int64`, which wire cannot supply, and the service no longer consumes `AnonStore`. `pkg/server/wire.go` is not updated in this PR. Wire generation will fail either on the unsatisfiable `int64` or on an unused provider, unless that registration is removed. Any other single-argument callers of `ProvideAnonDBStore` will also fail to compile.

New `device_limit` setting is undocumented and missing from the default/sample config

`[auth.anonymous] device_limit` is read here, but the PR adds no entry to `conf/defaults.ini` / `conf/sample.ini` and no documentation. Operators have no way to discover the option. Nothing tells them that 0 means unlimited, that devices are counted over a 30-day window, or that anonymous users over the limit are rejected at authentication.

`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` has no type annotation, so with strictNullChecks TypeScript infers the property type as `undefined` rather than `number | undefined`. It still satisfies `implements GrafanaConfig`, but consumers of `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` see a type that can never hold a number. The backend always sends an int64 (0 when unset), so the value is never actually undefined. Annotate it, e.g. `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`.

No test exercises the limit through `AnonDeviceService.TagDevice` / `Anonymous.Authenticate`. Such a test would have caught that the local cache lets a rejected device through on its next request.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback chain depends on per-site default_locale but the translation LRU cache ignores it

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds the fallback chain from `SiteSetting.default_locale`, which differs per site in multisite and can be changed by an admin at runtime. The process-wide LRU cache in `I18n.translate` (translate_accelerator.rb, `k = "#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`) is keyed only by key, requested locale and backend.

Scenario: a user on site A (default `de`) requests a key that is missing in `ja`. The `de` fallback string is cached. A `ja` user on site B (default `fr`) in the same process then gets site A's German text. The same staleness happens after an admin changes `default_locale`: earlier fallback results stay cached until the process restarts.

Fix: include the resolved fallback chain (or the site default locale) in the cache key, or skip caching results that came from a fallback.

Fallback locales are only loaded in ApplicationController, so other contexts miss fallbacks and can poison the cache

The patched loader only loads translation files on demand. `I18n.translate` loads `config.locale` only, and the fallback locales (site default and `:en`) are loaded only by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` in `ApplicationController#set_locale`. These paths never call it:
- Sidekiq jobs and mailers
- rake tasks
- controllers or middleware outside ApplicationController
- `I18n.t(..., locale: x)` calls

In those paths a key missing from the current locale falls back to locales whose translations were never loaded, so the lookup returns "translation missing: ...". For argument-less `I18n.t` calls that string is frozen into the shared LRU cache under `key+locale`. Later web requests get the cached "translation missing" text even after `ensure_loaded!` has loaded `en`.

Fix: load the fallback chain inside the patched `I18n.translate` / `load_locale`, not in a controller filter.

No specs for the new fallback behavior

The PR adds a custom fallback order (user locale → site default → en), changes the loading path (`ensure_loaded!`), and turns fallbacks on in every environment, including test and development. No tests cover any of it.

There is no check that:
- a key missing in the user locale resolves from the site default locale, then from English;
- the fallback locales get loaded;
- cached translations behave correctly when the default locale changes.

Regressions such as the cache and loading issues in this change would go unnoticed.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: EmbeddableHost's before_validation callback unconditionally calls self.host.sub!, causing NoMethodError when host is nil.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Migrated hosts are not normalized, silently breaking existing embeds

The old `allows_embeddable_host?` explicitly accepted entries like `http://eviltrout.com` and `https://...`; there were specs for this. The migration inserts each line of `embeddable_hosts` verbatim. It does not strip the scheme, path, whitespace or `\r` (CRLF input), and it does not skip blank lines.

The new lookup compares `lower(host)` against the bare `uri.host`. Rows such as `http://eviltrout.com` or `eviltrout.com\r` therefore never match. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: category_fabricator.rb and embeddable_host_fabricator.rb contain each other's fabricator definitions. The candidate describes different consequences but correctly identifies the swapped contents.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.

Raw string interpolation into INSERT SQL

Any stored value containing a single quote makes the migration fail with a SQL syntax error, and in general this is an injection-prone pattern. Use `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.quote(h)` or bind parameters.

Migration crashes when no embed_category setting row exists

The query joining `categories` to `site_settings` on `name = 'embed_category'` returns no rows when `embed_category` was never set. That is the default (`''` is not persisted), it is the state on every fresh install, and it also happens when the stored name no longer matches a category. Calling `[0]` on an empty PG::Result raises IndexError (and even if it returned nil, `['id']` would raise NoMethodError). So `rake db:migrate` aborts for most existing sites and all new installs. The validation explicitly allows an optional `:port`, and `before_validation` only strips the scheme and path, so `example.com:8080` is stored as is. `record_for_host` compares against `URI#host`, which never includes the port. Such a record is accepted by the UI but never authorizes any referer.

The server substitutes `uncategorized_category_id`, but the client sets `host.category` to `Discourse.Category.findById(null)`, which is undefined. The row shows no category until the page is reloaded. Use the `category_id` returned in the save response instead of the local `categoryId`.

For `*_ids` keys the code maps every id through `_lookupSubType`, which returns undefined when an id is not present in the sideloaded collection. The resulting array can contain undefined holes, so templates that iterate it (e.g. `embeddable-host` components) break. If the value is null, `obj[k].map` throws. The `hydrated || []` fallback does nothing because `map` always returns an array. Filter out missing entries and guard against non-array values.
