The test fetches `store.find('fruit', 2)` (banana, `color_ids: [3]`) but asserts two colors with ids 1 and 2. It passes only because the Pretender handler for `/fruits/:id` always returns `fruits[0]` (apple). The test does not check what it appears to, and it would fail if the fixture were fixed to respect the id.

Test name no longer matches the behavior under test

`expandable_first_post?` no longer depends on embeddable hosts at all, since the `embeddable_hosts.present?` check was removed. The spec "is false if embeddable_host is blank" now passes only because `embed_truncate` defaults to false and the topic has no embed. The `Fabricate(:embeddable_host)` in the nested before block is irrelevant. The spec gives false confidence about a host-based condition that no longer exists.

New admin endpoints have no behavioral tests

The specs for `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` and `Admin::EmbeddingController` only assert the class hierarchy. Nothing tests create/update/destroy, the defaulting of `category_id` to uncategorized, validation-error responses, or the serialized embedding payload. The bugs these specs would catch (nil handling, missing records) go undetected.

`category_id` is NOT NULL, but there is no foreign key, no validation that the category exists, and no cleanup when a category is deleted. Hosts can end up pointing at nonexistent categories: the admin UI badge is blank and imports silently go to uncategorized.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Match statistics are written inside validation, so they get double-counted or rolled back

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count` and saves the row. It is called from `EmailValidator#validate_each`, so it runs on every validation pass. The counts end up wrong in two ways.

1. Double counting: `UsersController#create` always calls `user.valid?` (line 168; the `&&` evaluates `valid?` first) and then `user.save` (line 172), which validates again. Every signup attempt for a `do_nothing` email is counted twice.
2. Lost counts: `save`/`save!` run validations inside the record's transaction and raise `ActiveRecord::Rollback` when validation fails. When the email is actually blocked, the increment made during `save` is rolled back. Paths that only call `save!` (e.g. `User.create_for_email` for invites) never record blocked matches at all.

The result is that `match_count`/`last_match_at` are inconsistent and unreliable, which is the stated purpose of these columns. Don't write to the database from inside a validator; record the match explicitly after the create attempt, outside the user's transaction.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: the email-blocking predicate updates match statistics during what should be a read-only check. The candidate details validation-related double counting and rollback consequences rather than race conditions or misleading naming, but the problematic side effect is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is an exact, case-sensitive match and is trivially bypassed

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` compares the raw submitted value. Neither the stored email nor the input is downcased or stripped. If `bad@spammers.org` is blocked, a spammer can register as `Bad@spammers.org` or `BAD@SPAMMERS.ORG` and pass validation. The uniqueness validation on `BlockedEmail.email` is also case-sensitive, so case-variant duplicates can be inserted. Normalize the email (e.g. `Email.downcase(email).strip`) both when storing and when looking up, or compare with `lower(email)`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-sensitive blocked-email lookup vulnerability, where changing an email's capitalization bypasses an existing block. The candidate's additional normalization and uniqueness concerns do not change the underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
match_count increment is a racy read-modify-write

`should_block?` loads the record, does `record.match_count += 1`, and then calls `record.save`. Concurrent signup attempts for the same email can read the same value and overwrite each other's increment, losing counts. Each save also triggers a uniqueness-validation query. Use an atomic update instead, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])`.

Any server-side email error permanently marks the address as 'invalid' on the client

The client pushes the email into `rejectedEmails` whenever `result.errors.email` is present. That includes errors like "has already been taken" or the domain whitelist/blacklist message, not only the new blocked-email error. From then on, the inline validation for that address shows the generic `user.email.invalid` text, which is misleading for the "already taken" case. The address also stays rejected for the rest of the page session, because `rejectedEmails` is never cleared.

No tests for the end-to-end blocking or the new create response fields

The specs only exercise `EmailValidator#validate_each` with `should_block?` stubbed, and `BlockedEmail.should_block?` in isolation. Nothing verifies that `User` actually rejects a blocked email through `valid?`/`save`. Nothing covers the new `errors`/`values` keys in the `UsersController#create` failure response that the JS now depends on, or the match-count behavior through the real controller flow. The double-count and rollback problems in `should_block?` would have been caught by such tests.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy-prefix mixins pass modern values verbatim to old-spec properties with different semantics

`align-items($alignment)` copies its argument into `-webkit-box-align` and `-ms-flex-align`. Those legacy properties accept `start`/`end`, not `flex-start`/`flex-end`, so any future caller using those values emits invalid declarations for the browsers the prefixes target. `-ms-align-items` is not a real property and is dead output.

`order($val)` has the same problem: `-webkit-box-ordinal-group`/`-moz-box-ordinal-group` are 1-based (default 1, values must be >= 1), while `order` defaults to 0. As a result, `order(0)` or negative values are invalid in the legacy model, and `order(1)` orders elements differently in legacy vs. modern browsers.

The current callers (center, baseline, 2, 3) happen to work. The mixins should map the values, or document that they only accept safe values.

Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

ActiveModel::Serializers looks for `include_<attr>?` predicates. This method is named `include_website_name` without the `?`, so the serializer never calls it. `website_name` is therefore always emitted (as `null` when there is no website), and any intended gating does not happen.

The new `website_name` attribute was added to the plain `attributes` list but not to `untrusted_attributes`, so it is always serialized. For instances hosted on shared domains this gives wrong results. For example, an instance at `forum.trydiscourse.com` (or `x.herokuapp.com`, `x.github.io`, `forum.co.uk`) will show the full URL path for any user website like `spam.trydiscourse.com/...` or `other.co.uk/...`. The new `website_name` specs only exercise the identical-host, different-host and parent-domain cases. Nothing tests the `www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com` branch, a blank website, or a website without a path. The most complex conditional in the method is effectively untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kernel#open on admin-supplied feed URL allows command execution / local file read

`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` relies on open-uri's patched `Kernel#open`. That only does an HTTP fetch when the string looks like a `scheme://` URL; otherwise it falls back to plain `Kernel#open`. A value like `|some shell command` runs a subprocess, and `/etc/passwd` reads a local file whose content is then imported as a public topic. The URL is never validated, so an admin (not necessarily a server operator on hosted installs) gets RCE or file disclosure. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unvalidated SiteSetting.feed_polling_url passed to open. The candidate emphasizes command execution and local file disclosure rather than arbitrary URL fetching, but points to the same unsafe input handling and call site.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring match

`discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` accepts any origin that is a prefix of `discourseUrl`. For example, `http://forum.example.co` passes when discourseUrl is `http://forum.example.com/`. A foreign origin can then send `discourse-resize` messages. Compare `e.origin` exactly against the origin parsed from `discourseUrl`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying vulnerability: using indexOf for postMessage origin validation permits unintended origins through substring matching. The different example domains do not change the issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.

The post is then stored with `cook_method: raw_html`, so it is never sanitized. Anyone can trigger this by calling `/embed/best?embed_url=...` with a spoofed Referer, which leaves a script-bearing post on the forum domain. `<%- end if %>` typo turns the if/else into a modifier conditional

`end if` makes the whole if/else block a trailing `if` modifier whose condition is the next compiled ERB statement (the output-buffer append for the following text). The template only renders because that append happens to be truthy. Output is also reordered: the condition is evaluated before the block. This should be a plain `<%- end %>`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same nil-content crash caused by calling `i.content.scrub` when RSS items lack content, and recommends falling back to description. The additional Ruby-version concern does not negate the match.

false_positives.candidate:
raw_html cook method bypasses all HTML sanitization for imported content

When `cook_method == raw_html`, `cook` returns `raw` verbatim and skips the normal pipeline that sanitizes HTML. Imported content reaches it unfiltered from two places. The RSS job uses `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content)`, so `<script>`, `on*` handlers and `<iframe>` from the feed are stored. The Readability import whitelists `href`/`src` attributes, so `javascript:` URLs pass through. That HTML is rendered as-is in the forum and in the embed view (`raw post.cooked`). Any third-party or compromised content in the feed or blog becomes stored XSS on the Discourse origin. The imported HTML should still be run through a sanitizer/whitelist.

Unauthenticated callers can create unlimited topics by varying the embed URL

Any request with a matching Referer (trivially spoofed outside a browser) enqueues `retrieve_topic` for an arbitrary `embed_url`. The only throttle, in `TopicRetriever#retrieved_recently?`, is keyed on the exact URL string. Adding a different query string (`?a=1`, `?a=2`, ...) on the embeddable host therefore bypasses it. Each variant causes a server-side fetch and, if the host returns 200, a new topic via `import_remote`. The job is also enqueued on every hit, including the loading page's 30-second auto-reload. Consider normalizing URLs, rate limiting per IP, and limiting how many new embeds can be created.

The checks `href.start_with?('/')` and `src.start_with?('/')` also match protocol-relative URLs like `//cdn.example.com/img.png`. `sub(/^\/+/, '')` then strips both slashes and produces `http://bloghost/cdn.example.com/img.png`. Protocol-relative image and CDN links are common in blog/RSS content, so they will be broken in imported posts. Skip values starting with `//`, or resolve properly with `URI.join(url, href)`. The same bug exists in the `img` branch at line 70.

Crash when the embedded post has been deleted

`post = embed.post` returns nil if a moderator deleted the imported post, because Trashable's default scope hides it. When the feed content later changes, `PostRevisor.new(nil).revise!` raises NoMethodError. `PollFeed` loops over all items without rescue, so one deleted embed aborts processing of every later feed item on every hourly run. Handle a missing post explicitly, e.g. skip it or clean up the embed.

TopicEmbed created from a failed post leads to NOT NULL violation

`PostCreator#create` returns the post object even when saving failed and rolled back; the post then has `errors` and `id`/`topic_id` are nil. `post.present?` is still true, so `TopicEmbed.create!(topic_id: nil, post_id: nil, ...)` runs. The model validations only check `embed_url`/`content_sha1`, so this reaches the DB and raises on the NOT NULL columns. Check `post.persisted?` / `post.errors.blank?` before creating the embed.

The throttle calls `setnx` and then `expire` in a separate command. If the process dies or Redis errors between the two calls, the key never expires and that embed URL is treated as 'retrieved recently' forever. Use a single atomic `SET key 1 NX EX 60`.

When feed polling is enabled, each cache miss calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline. That downloads the whole feed and runs `TopicEmbed.import` for every item. Together with the per-URL throttle (bypassable via distinct URLs), requests for unknown URLs can repeatedly trigger full feed downloads and imports.

Disqus import loses --category and thread dates and now depends on live HTTP fetches

The `--category` option was removed, so existing invocations that pass `-c` will fail. Topics are no longer created with the thread's original `created_at`. Each thread now calls `import_remote`, which fetches the link over the network. Any 404/timeout raises OpenURI::HTTPError and aborts the whole import. Non-http links make `import` return nil, so those threads are silently skipped.

URL/username requirement specs pass trivially

`feed_polling_enabled` defaults to false and is not stubbed to true in the 'requires feed_polling_url' and 'requires embed_by_username' examples. `poll_feed` is therefore never called no matter what the URL or username checks do, so these tests do not verify the conditions they describe. true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

Dayjs objects compared with `===`, so the 'unavailable all day' branch never runs

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two freshly created object references, so it is always false. Overrides that mark a day unavailable (start == end) never take this early-reject path.

The later checks miss a slot starting exactly at the override instant (midnight in the organizer's zone), because `slotStartTime.isAfter(end)` is false for equal times. Since `dateOverrideExist` is then true, the function returns true and also skips the busy check. A slot at midnight on a day the host marked unavailable can therefore be offered. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: === compares Dayjs object references rather than date values, making the comparison always false. The candidate also recommends .isSame(), matching the golden fix.

On any day with a date override, the user's existing Cal bookings and connected-calendar busy times are therefore ignored. All users of a non-team event count as fixed hosts, so this affects personal event types too, not only round-robin. Invitees can book slots that overlap existing bookings or calendar events.

Only the working-hours check should be skipped when an override exists. The busy check must still run.

Working-hours check rejects every slot when a user has more than one working-hours entry for a day

`workingHours.find(...)` returns true, and the slot is rejected, if the slot falls outside ANY working-hours entry that includes the slot's UTC weekday. It should only reject when the slot is inside none of them.

`getWorkingHours` splits ranges that cross UTC midnight into two entries with shifted `days`. Example: a PST user working Mon–Fri 9–17 gets {days 1–5, 1020–1439} and {days 2–6, 0–60}.
- A Tuesday 18:00Z slot fits the first entry but is outside the second, so it is rejected.
- A Tuesday 00:30Z slot is rejected by the first entry.

The logic should accept a slot that fits within at least one applicable entry.

Multiple date-override ranges on the same day reject all slots

`dateOverrides.find` returns true, and the slot is marked unavailable, as soon as ANY override on the slot's day doesn't contain the slot.

Date overrides support several time ranges per day (e.g. 9–10 and 14–15). A slot in the first range is outside the second, and vice versa, so every slot on that day is rejected for the fixed host. The check should reject only when the slot is outside ALL override ranges for that day.

The code checks whether the slot is on the override's day by comparing the UTC date of the override's real start instant with the slot's UTC date. A date override covers a calendar day in the organizer's timezone.

Example: a PST organizer sets an override for day D 16:00–20:00, i.e. D+1 00:00Z–04:00Z. The real start falls on UTC day D+1.
- Slots during the organizer's day D (e.g. D 17:00Z = 09:00 PST) don't match, so normal working hours apply and they are wrongly offered.
- Slots on UTC day D+1 (a normal day for the organizer) match and are wrongly rejected as outside the override.

If shifting by `inviteeOffset - organizerOffset` pushes the override across the invitee's midnight, `endTime` wraps below `startTime`. Example: a UTC override 16:00–22:00 for an IST invitee becomes 21:30 → 1290 and 03:30 → 210.

`buildSlots` skips any boundary with `start >= end`, so the whole override vanishes. The user's working hours for that day have already been removed, so the invitee sees no slots at all from that host. The range needs to be split at midnight, or clamped to the invitee's day.

`override.start` holds the organizer's wall-clock time stored as UTC. The filter `dayjs.utc(override.start).isBetween(startOfInviteeDay, ...)` compares that naive value with real instants of the invitee's day, without converting it.

Example: an IST override on D 15:00–18:00 (real D 09:30Z = 19:30 Brisbane on D). For a Brisbane (+10) invitee the naive D T15:00Z falls in invitee day D+1.

- The host's normal working hours are removed on D+1.
- Day D keeps the normal working hours.

Any caller of `getSlots` that passes overrides without `timeZone` now gets them shifted by `inviteeOffset - serverLocalOffset`. Previously they were used as-is, so results now depend on the server or client machine timezone. Either require `timeZone` or skip the shift when it is absent.

Transient failures permanently delete reminders after two cron runs

The catch block increments `retryCount` for any exception in the try body. That includes transient errors such as Twilio 5xx or 429 rate limits, network timeouts, the `prisma.profile.findFirst` or `getBookerBaseUrl` calls, and template rendering. It also includes the `scheduled: true` update failing after Twilio already accepted the message.

After two failures the row is deleted on the next run. Previously the reminder would be retried until its scheduled date (up to 7 days out). Now a short Twilio or DB outage spanning two cron invocations silently and permanently drops every SMS reminder processed during it.

If the post-schedule update is what failed, the reminder is retried and deleted while a Twilio message is already queued. That causes duplicate sends, and the `referenceId` needed to cancel the queued message is lost.

Only known-permanent errors (e.g. Twilio invalid-number error codes) should count toward deletion, or the retry budget should be larger or time-based.

SMS-locked users/teams have their reminders deleted

`twilio.scheduleSMS` returns `undefined`, not an error, when the user or team has `smsLockState === LOCKED`. This new `else` branch treats that as a failed attempt and increments `retryCount`, so after two cron runs every pending SMS reminder for that account is deleted.

Previously these reminders stayed unscheduled and would be sent if an admin unlocked the account, for example after a false-positive abuse lock. Now unlocking does not restore them and attendees silently get no reminders.

The locked case should be distinguished from a real scheduling failure.

Failure inside the catch handler aborts the whole cron run

The catch block now awaits `prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` before logging. If that update throws, the exception escapes the `for` loop and the handler. This happens for example when the original error was a DB connectivity problem, or when the row was deleted concurrently (e.g. a booking cancellation), which makes Prisma throw `P2025`.

All remaining reminders in the batch are then skipped, the endpoint returns 500, and the original error is never logged. Before this PR the catch only logged, so one bad reminder could not stop the rest.

Wrap the counter update in its own try/catch, or log first and ignore update failures.

Reminders with no recipient or empty message are still retried indefinitely

The PR's goal is to stop endlessly re-processing reminders that can never be sent. However, when `sendTo` is null (e.g. `smsReminderNumber` missing) or the rendered message is empty, the `if` at this line is skipped. Neither branch increments `retryCount`, so these reminders are still re-fetched and fully re-processed on every cron run until their scheduled date. That includes the profile lookup, booker-URL resolution and template rendering. These permanently unsendable cases are arguably the ones that most need the retry cap.

No tests for the new retry/deletion behavior

The PR adds behavior that deletes user-facing reminders, but no tests cover it. Cases worth testing: incrementing `retryCount` on a falsy `scheduleSMS` result and on thrown errors, deleting reminders with `retryCount > 1`, leaving reminders of other methods untouched, and not deleting on success. Given the data-loss risk if the conditions are wrong, these should be covered.

false_positives.candidate:
Top-level OR fragments are returned without outer parentheses, so composing them gives wrong results

`Prisma.sql` inlines nested fragments verbatim; it does not wrap them in parentheses. Several public methods return a fragment whose top level is an unparenthesized OR:
- `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` / `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` return `(A AND B) OR (C AND D)`.
- `buildFilterConditions` returns `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` when only one filter is set.
- `getBaseConditions` returns the auth fragment bare when there are no filters.

These methods are the replacement for `findMany`, so callers must embed the fragments in their own queries. A natural pattern is `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "createdAt" >= ${start}`. That parses as `(team branch) OR ((user branch) AND createdAt >= start)`, so date, status or any other extra predicate applies to only one branch. The result is wrong counts and leaked rows outside the requested range.

It is worse with `getFilterConditions()`: `WHERE ${auth} AND ${filter}` becomes `... OR "eventParentId" = X`, which returns rows with that eventParentId regardless of authorization.

The old Prisma where-object API could not be mis-composed this way. Each returned fragment should be wrapped in parentheses, e.g. `Prisma.sql\`(${...})\``, so it is safe to combine.

Public `findMany` method removed and constructor contract changed

The public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method is deleted and replaced with `getBaseConditions()`, which returns a raw SQL fragment. All getters now return `Prisma.Sql` instead of `BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedWhereInput`.

Existing callers of `findMany` or of `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions` would break. That includes any code passing the conditions into a Prisma `where`. Those callers would get type errors or, if typed loosely, runtime query failures.

Only the test file is updated in this PR. The PR also says the type-check and test runner were not run successfully. Either confirm there are no other consumers or migrate them in this PR.

Caching tests deleted although caching logic remains

The entire `Caching` describe block was removed, covering both authorization and filter condition caching. The service still caches through `cachedAuthConditions` and `cachedFilterConditions`.

The cache uses an `=== undefined` sentinel, and `null` is a valid cached filter value. Without these tests, a regression in that logic would go unnoticed. The tests only needed their expectations updated to `Prisma.sql` values, not removal.

Minimum token schema strips every field except access_token

`[z.string().toString()]` is not a pattern key. `ZodString.toString()` returns "[object Object]", so both computed keys are the same literal property "[object Object]" and the second overwrites the first. The effective schema is `{access_token: string, "[object Object]"?: unknown}` in zod's default strip mode. In sync mode every other property is therefore dropped: expiry_date, expires_in, scope, token_type, instance_url, etc. The consequences differ per app. Zoom computes `expiry_date` from an undefined `expires_in` (NaN, stored as null), so the next `zoomTokenSchema.parse` fails. Salesforce loses `instance_url`. Google loses `expiry_date`, `scope` and `token_type`. Use `.passthrough()` or `z.record`/`.catchall` with an explicit expiry field.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

After the first refresh, the next `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in the constructor throws, and the Google Calendar integration stops working for that user. - HubSpot treats the result as a token object (`expiresIn`, `accessToken`), computes a NaN expiry and stores the Response object as the credential key.

false_positives.candidate:
appStoreMetadata is indexed by slug, but it is keyed by app directory name

`appStoreMetadata` is generated keyed by app directory name (e.g. `googlecalendar`, `zoomvideo`, `office365calendar`), not by slug. Looking it up with `app.slug` (`google-calendar`, `zoom`, `office365-calendar`, `msteams`) returns undefined, so the webhook answers 404 for most of the OAuth apps this PR targets. It only works by accident where slug equals dirName. Select `dirName` from the App row and index by that.

`prisma` used without being imported

The new `prisma.credential.update(...)` call references `prisma`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. At best it resolves to the dev-only `globalThis.prisma`. In production that global is not set, so this throws a ReferenceError/TypeError. Since `getClient` runs in the constructor, every Salesforce booking/CRM operation fails.

Zoom sends app slug "zoomvideo" instead of "zoom"

Zoom's app slug and appId is "zoom" (see `createOAuthAppCredential({ appId: "zoom" ...})` in the callback). The webhook also identifies apps by slug. The refresh call sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, the directory name, so the self-hoster's sync endpoint gets an identifier that doesn't match what it uses for the webhook. Zoom refreshes will fail or return the wrong app's tokens.

Webex, Lark and MS Teams still require the provider-native response shape in sync mode

Webex validates the response with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` directly, which requires a scope literal, token_type, refresh_token and refresh_token_expires_in. Lark runs it through `handleLarkError`, which expects `{code:0,data:{...}}`. MS Teams overwrites the entire stored key with the response. All three are routed to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, whose documented contract is "only the access token and expiry date". With a conforming endpoint, Webex rejects every refresh, Lark throws, and Teams loses its refresh_token. The endpoint contract is not consistent across the integrations this PR switches over.

Outbound sync request carries no authentication

Cal.com POSTs only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` to the sync endpoint, with no shared secret, signature or encryption. The inbound webhook, by contrast, requires a secret and AES-encrypted keys. The self-hoster's endpoint therefore has no way to verify that the caller is Cal.com. Anyone who can reach it can enumerate user ids and obtain live third-party access tokens. Send the webhook secret or an HMAC header, and ideally encrypt the response with the shared key. Also check `response.ok` before returning.

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`

The secret is compared with `!==`, which leaks timing information. If the header is sent more than once it becomes a `string[]` and never matches. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on the buffers after checking the lengths. The endpoint also accepts any HTTP method.

Updating a credential via the webhook doesn't clear `invalid`

Google, Zoom and Webex set `invalid: true` on invalid_grant. When the parent app later pushes fresh keys through this webhook, only `key` is updated. The credential stays flagged invalid and is still treated as broken. Reset `invalid: false` on update.

Removed diagnostic logging of the Microsoft refresh error

The old code logged the zod error and the raw Microsoft response when parsing failed. Now `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws a generic "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" and the MS error body is lost. That makes Outlook token problems much harder to debug. The behavior also changed from "keep the old token and continue" to "throw".

No tests for the new refresh/sync helpers or the webhook

The PR changes token refresh for about ten integrations and adds a credential-writing webhook, and it states that no tests were added or run. Unit tests for `parseRefreshTokenResponse` would have caught several of the issues above: the returned wrapper object, the fields stripped by the broken schema, and the placeholder refresh_token. The same goes for `refreshOAuthTokens` (sync vs native return types) and the webhook (slug→metadata lookup).

If it was already `cancelled: true` (from `requestReschedule`), or is later marked cancelled by a workflow edit, the cron sends a second cancel for the same batch.

false_positives.candidate:
One failed SendGrid cancel aborts the whole cancellation batch on every cron run

One `try` wraps the entire `for` loop of `client.request` calls, and the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` promises run only at the end via `Promise.all`. Prisma promises are lazy, so if any cancel request throws, the loop stops and none of the queued deletes execute.

This includes reminders that SendGrid already cancelled earlier in the same run. They keep `cancelled: true`, so the next run re-POSTs a cancel for those batch ids. SendGrid can reject a cancel for a batch that is already cancelled, and that failure aborts the loop again.

Concrete triggers:
- the 100 pending-cancellation limit;
- a batch already cancelled through the `immediateDelete` path (e.g. organizer `requestReschedule` sets `cancelled=true`, then the attendee reschedules and `handleNewBooking` cancels the same batch immediately);
- a null `referenceId`.

One bad row therefore blocks every other cancellation until its `scheduledDate` passes, and those other emails are sent. Handle each reminder in its own try/catch and delete or mark each row right after its own request succeeds.

Workflow/step deletion still cancels immediately and is subject to the 100-cancellation limit

When a workflow is deleted (and when a step is deleted, line 521), every scheduled email reminder is cancelled with `immediateDelete=true`. That issues one SendGrid scheduled_sends cancel per reminder right away.

A workflow active on many event types can easily have more than 100 scheduled reminders in the 72h window. Past the account-wide limit, the remaining cancels fail. The failures are only logged inside `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`, and the rows are then cascade-deleted with the workflow or step, so nothing retries. Those reminders are still delivered after the user deleted the workflow.

This path needs its own deferred mechanism, for example detaching or keeping cancelled rows instead of cascade-deleting them before the cron processes them.

Deferring cancellation for imminent reminders can miss SendGrid's cancel cutoff

Every cancellation with a `referenceId` is now deferred to the cron by setting `cancelled: true`, whatever the reminder's `scheduledDate`. The cron runs every 15 minutes, and SendGrid only honours a scheduled-send cancel made at least ~10 minutes before send time.

If a booking is cancelled or rescheduled roughly 10–25 minutes before its reminder is due, the cron may not run before the cutoff, so the email goes out. The previous immediate cancel would have stopped it.

Cancel immediately when `scheduledDate` is already inside the cron's 1-hour window; only reminders further out need to be deferred.

`Prisma` is still imported from `@prisma/client`, but its only use was in the removed `PrismaPromise<Prisma.BatchPayload>[]` arrays, so it is now unused. The import also lost its trailing comma.

This will trip lint (no-unused-vars) and formatting checks.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Hung flusher processes are never killed, so a duplicate flusher is started for the same shards

The kill is now guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. Real processes are created with `self.mp_context.Process`, i.e. `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess` directly, not `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`), so the check is always False and `process.kill()` never runs.

The old code called `kill()` unconditionally. Now, when a process is detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`), it keeps running and `_create_process_for_shards` spawns a second process for the same shards. Both processes share the same `stopped`, `healthy_since` and `backpressure_since` Values.

Consequences:
- Two flushers can flush the same shards concurrently, which risks duplicate segments on buffered-segments.
- Processes leak on every restart, up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process index.
- A recovered zombie keeps updating the shared health and backpressure values.

Fix: check against `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` or the concrete `SpawnProcess` class, or test `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

It correctly concludes that hung flusher processes are never killed and explains the resulting duplicate-process behavior.

Diff-trimming logic can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of reporting the error The `start` and `end` loops that trim common prefix and suffix are computed independently. Neither is bounded by `length - start`, so they can overlap. Example 1: value `y` sanitizes to `y`. That gives start=1 and end=8, and `sanitized.substring(1, 0)` throws. Example 2: value `x` sanitizes to `x`. That gives start=11 and end=4, and `value.substring(11, 7)` throws. The unchecked exception escapes `verify()`, which only catches IOException. The Maven build then fails with a stack trace instead of the intended `Illegal HTML in key ...` message. The end loop should be bounded, e.g. `end < Math.min(value.length(), sanitized.length()) - start`.

Anchor mismatch message omits key and file, making failures hard to locate

`santizeAnchors` receives `key` but never uses it. It reports only `Didn't find anchor tag <a ...> in original string`.

When the verifier runs across dozens of message files, a failing build gives no indication of which file or key is at fault. By contrast, the `Illegal HTML` message includes both. The key and `file` should be included in this message.

ANCHOR_PATTERN matches any tag starting with 'a', not just anchors

`</?a[^>]*>` also matches `<abbr>`, `<area ...>`, `<audio ...>`, `<article>`, `<aside>`, etc. Any such tag in the English source string is treated as an "anchor" and stripped before sanitization. An identical tag in a translation is therefore accepted without going through the OWASP policy, including any attributes such as event handlers. Non-anchor tags in translations are also misreported as anchor mismatches.

The pattern should be restricted to real anchors, e.g. `</?a(?:\s[^>]*)?>`.

false_positives.candidate:
Session type is wrong for the first access token issued with offline_access

The session type is taken from `userSession.isOffline()`. In the code-to-token and password grants with `scope=offline_access`, the access token is created from the online user session before `generateRefreshToken()` creates the offline session.

As a result, that access token is encoded as `on` (online). Right afterwards the online session is removed: always in `ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType`, and when `FIRST_OFFLINE_ACCESS` is set in `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse`. The token then advertises an online session that no longer exists; the session survives only as offline.

The stated purpose is to look up only the encoded session type (#37662). Any such consumer would fail to find the session and reject a valid token. Use `clientSessionContext.isOfflineTokenRequested()` (or equivalent) to decide between offline and online.

Grant type only recorded for grants that go through createTokenResponse; client_credentials (and UMA) end up as 'na'

`Constants.GRANT_TYPE` is set on the client session context only in `createTokenResponse`, plus explicitly in ROPC, pre-authorized code, refresh and standard token exchange.

`ClientCredentialsGrantType` builds its response via `tokenManager.responseBuilder(...).generateAccessToken()` without calling `createTokenResponse`, and this PR does not change it. The permission (UMA) grant also does not use `createTokenResponse`.

Tokens from these grants are therefore encoded with the unknown grant `na`, even though shortcuts `cc` and `pg` were added to their factories. This silently defeats the feature for the client-credentials case. No test catches it, because `expectClientLogin` does not check `TOKEN_ID`.

New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing custom grant type factories at startup

`getShortcut()` is added to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` without a default implementation.

Any custom `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` compiled against the previous SPI will throw `AbstractMethodError` when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` calls `gtf.getShortcut()`, which prevents server startup. A custom implementation returning `null` would instead cause an NPE from `ConcurrentHashMap.put`.

Consider a default implementation (or a fallback to `na`) and handling of null shortcuts instead of failing boot.

Javadoc recommends 3-letter shortcuts, but encoding/decoding requires exactly 2 characters with no validation

The Javadoc says the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters". However, `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId` hard-codes a 6-character prefix and takes characters 4-6 as the grant shortcut.

A custom grant that follows the doc and returns a 3-letter shortcut will produce token ids (e.g. `onrtabc:...`) that the same provider cannot decode; it throws "Expected length of 6".

Neither `postInit` nor the lazy refresh paths in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory` validate shortcut length. The doc should say exactly 2 characters, and the factory should reject other lengths.

Public copy constructor Context(Context) removed from SPI class

The public `OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context)` copy constructor is deleted rather than updated to copy the new `grantType` field.

Custom grant implementations or wrappers that used it to derive or modify a context will fail to compile or link. This removal is unrelated to the feature, which only needed the new field copied. Keep the constructor and copy `grantType` in it.

Lazy map refresh can silently overwrite existing shortcut mappings

`postInit` detects duplicate shortcuts by comparing map sizes. The lazy refresh in `getShortcutByGrantType` and `getGrantTypeByShortcut` instead blindly `put`s into both maps.

A newly deployed grant whose shortcut collides with an existing one would overwrite the mapping in `grantsByShortcuts`. Previously issued tokens would then decode to the wrong grant type, and the two maps would become inconsistent. The two maps are also updated non-atomically.

The refresh paths should apply the same collision and length validation, e.g. via `putIfAbsent` and rejecting conflicts.

Access token jti is no longer a UUID

The access token `jti` changes from a 36-char UUID to a prefixed form, e.g. `onrtac:<uuid>`, 43 chars containing `:`.

Resource servers or integrations that parse or validate `jti` as a UUID, or store it in fixed-length/UUID-typed columns for replay detection, will break after upgrade. This externally visible format change is not documented in upgrade/migration notes in this PR.

A symmetric bug in the encoder and decoder would pass.

The test should generate keys on the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and assert `assertArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des)` and/or verify the re-encoded signature.

So the advertised feature can never return results and turns any crafted cursor like `0:-5:0` into an unhandled 500. The comment claiming the ORM 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. The comment saying this gives 'access to data beyond normal pagination bounds' describes an intent that should not ship. Negative offsets should be rejected with BadPaginationError (as OffsetPaginator does), not passed through.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Narrowed lock lets concurrent builds of the same key run in parallel and overwrite each other

`getOrCreateIndex` checks `GetIndex` and then calls `BuildIndex` with no per-key guard. With the function-wide lock removed, a Search request and a watch event for the same uncached key can build two indexes at once.

The last `b.cache[key] = idx` wins. Any watch-event writes already applied to the losing index are discarded. `IndexTenants` is also incremented twice. For file-backed indexes, the second `bleve.New` on the same directory fails.

Fix: re-check the cache under the write lock before storing, or use a per-key singleflight so finer-grained locking does not introduce lost updates.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race: narrowing the lock lets multiple goroutines build the same uncached key concurrently, then the final cache write overwrites earlier results and loses updates.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

New TotalDocs() log call can crash the process via unsynchronized map iteration

The new log line calls `s.search.TotalDocs()`. By then the goroutine at lines 207-213 is already consuming watch events. `bleveBackend.TotalDocs` (bleve.go:146) ranges over `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu`.

A watch event for a namespace that has no index yet goes through `handleEvent` -> `getOrCreateIndex` -> `BuildIndex`, which writes `b.cache[key]` under `cacheMu.Lock()`. That write can overlap with the lock-free iteration in `TotalDocs`. Concurrent map iteration and write is a fatal Go runtime error, so it crashes the process; it is not a recoverable panic.

The window is roughly as long as `DocCount()` takes across all indexes. Namespaces skipped at startup because they are below `initMinSize` make this path reachable.

Fix: have `TotalDocs` take `cacheMu.RLock()`, or compute the total before starting the watch goroutine.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without cacheMu while the already-started watch goroutine can trigger BuildIndex writes to b.cache, causing a fatal concurrent map read/write. The proposed fixes also align.

false_positives.candidate:
Stop() no longer prevents requests from being served after shutdown

Before this PR, every handler (Create, Read, List, Watch, Search, IsHealthy, blob calls, etc.) called `s.Init(ctx)` and returned `s.initErr`. Since the `sync.Once` had already run, that meant returning whatever `Stop()` had stored ("service is stopping" / "service is stopped").

This PR removes all those calls, so `Stop()` writing `s.initErr` no longer has any effect. After `Stop()` cancels the server context and stops the backend lifecycle, handlers keep running against a stopped backend and a cancelled broadcaster. Callers no longer get a clear "service is stopped" error.

Fix: add an explicit stopped/ready check in the handlers, or have `Stop` close the gRPC service, instead of relying on the now-unused `initErr`.

Index-build goroutines race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed`, so errors can be lost

Each goroutine started by `group.Go` does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`; `return err`. Both variables are the outer function's locals and are shared by all workers.

Before this PR, `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its whole body, which largely serialized builds. With the lock narrowed, the builds now run truly in parallel. Two consequences:
- The race detector will flag it.
- One goroutine can overwrite another's error with nil before it is returned. A failed namespace build can then be silently dropped instead of failing startup as the comment on `init` promises.
- `namespaced_indexed` will be miscounted.

Fix: use a goroutine-local `err :=` and an `atomic.Int64` for the counter.

Failed Init in constructor leaks the cancel func and the already-initialized backend

When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()` or `s.lifecycle.Stop`.

If `lifecycle.Init` succeeded (for example, the DB connection was opened) and then `search.init` or `initWatcher` failed, the backend's resources and any pollers started are never cleaned up. The caller has no handle to clean them up either, because the server is returned as nil.

The same error is also logged twice: once inside `Init` and again here.

Integration test skipped for postgres instead of fixed, possibly masking a regression from eager init

This PR makes unified storage initialize (DB init, full index build, watchers) synchronously inside `NewResourceServer`, which changes storage-server startup behavior. In the same PR, the only module-server integration test is disabled for postgres with "not working in Drone. Works locally."

If the failure is caused by the new eager initialization (for example, slower startup or blocking DB init beyond the 500ms sleep), skipping the test hides exactly the regression the PR description asks reviewers about. Nothing else in the PR adds coverage for the new init-at-construction behavior.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close() shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, so every message after the first rebalance is dropped and committed

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, and every strategy returned by `create_with_partitions` gets the same instance (result_consumer.py:133 and :255). On any partition revocation, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the current strategy. That calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets every worker's `shutdown` flag, calls `Queue.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the workers.

On the next assignment, arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` again and the new strategy wraps the same dead pool. Each `submit` then goes through `FixedQueuePool.submit`: `add_offset` succeeds, but `work_queue.put` raises `queue.ShutDown`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches that exception and marks the offset completed, so the commit thread commits it.

Result: after the first rebalance (deploy, scale event, pod restart), no uptime result is processed, yet all offsets are committed. This is silent data loss.

The shared `OffsetTracker` makes it worse. Stale outstanding or committable offsets for revoked partitions survive into the new assignment. They can block commits forever, or be passed to arroyo's `stage_offsets` for unassigned partitions; that raises, and the whole commit batch fails every tick.

Fix: the pool and tracker should be owned per strategy, or reset on assignment. `close()` should not tear down a resource owned by the factory.

Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which ends up in arroyo's `StreamProcessor` commit callback. That callback calls `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets`/`commit_offsets` and updates the commit-policy state. Arroyo expects it to be called only from the processing thread, inside `submit`/`poll`/`join`. Here it runs concurrently with the main thread's `consumer.poll()` and with rebalance callbacks, with no synchronization.

Consequences:
- Races on arroyo's unsynchronized internal state (staged offsets, policy timestamps).
- Exceptions when staging offsets for partitions that were just revoked.
- Commits with `force=False` under `ONCE_PER_SECOND` may only be staged. Because the loop calls commit only when new offsets become committable, the trailing offsets can sit staged indefinitely once traffic pauses.

The committable offsets should be computed and committed from `poll()` on the main thread, as arroyo's `CommitOffsets` step does. `join()` should do a final forced commit.

Unbounded queues mean no backpressure, despite the docstring's claim

Each worker queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`. `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`, so arroyo never pauses the consumer. If processing is slower than ingestion (slow DB or cache, one hot queue), the consumer keeps reading the topic into memory. Every message, with its full `Message` object, is held in `WorkItem`, and the `OffsetTracker` sets grow alongside.

This can OOM the consumer. Because commits stay behind the slowest item, a crash also forces reprocessing of a very large backlog.

The class docstring (line 253) promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which is not true. Bound the queues, and raise `MessageRejected` from `submit` when the target queue is full.

join() ignores its timeout, shutdown blocks up to 5s per worker, and no final commit is made

`join(timeout)` discards the timeout and calls `close()`. `close()` waits up to 5s for the commit thread. It then calls `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`, which calls `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` on each worker in turn. With the default of 20 queues and workers stuck in slow processing, a rebalance or shutdown can block for about 100s, regardless of arroyo's `join_timeout`. That risks exceeding `max.poll.interval.ms` and triggering further rebalances.

`terminate()`, which is meant to be immediate, also goes through the same blocking `pool.shutdown()`.

In addition, the commit thread is stopped before the workers finish, and no final commit is issued. Offsets completed since the last 1s tick are never committed and will be reprocessed after every rebalance.

`test_offset_gaps_block_commits` (and `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` in the uptime tests) assert that a missing offset 101 prevents committing past 100.

The tracker does not keep blocking. After committing 100, `mark_committed` prunes `all_offsets` to {102, 103}. On the next tick, `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` jumps to 102, and the tracker commits 103 without 101 ever arriving.

The unit test only reaches 103 on its second wait because of this, not because 101 was submitted. The uptime test passes only because it stops observing before the second 1s tick.

Every processed item emits `metrics.gauge("remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth", ...)` in the worker's `finally` block. On a high-volume topic like uptime results, that is one statsd call per message per worker.

The gauge is tagged only with `identifier`, not with the worker or queue id. The values reported by different workers therefore overwrite each other, and the metric does not show any particular queue's depth.

`poll()` already reports total queue depth; per-queue depth could be emitted there, tagged by queue index.

Only the first request from a new device over the limit is rejected. For the next ~29 minutes (cache TTL), `localCache.Get(key)` hits, `tagDeviceUI` returns nil, and `Anonymous.Authenticate` lets the device in. The device is never stored or counted, so a user who just reloads the page is admitted. The cache entry should only be set after a successful create/update, or removed on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`.

`ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` used to receive `anonstore.AnonStore` via dependency injection, so a provider for it (`anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` plus a bind) was registered in the wire set. `ProvideAnonDBStore` now requires an `int64`, which wire cannot supply, and the service no longer consumes `AnonStore`. `pkg/server/wire.go` is not updated in this PR. false_positives.candidate:
Fallback chain depends on per-site default_locale but the translation LRU cache ignores it

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds the fallback chain from `SiteSetting.default_locale`, which differs per site in multisite and can be changed by an admin at runtime. The process-wide LRU cache in `I18n.translate` (translate_accelerator.rb, `k = "#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`) is keyed only by key, requested locale and backend.

Scenario: a user on site A (default `de`) requests a key that is missing in `ja`. The `de` fallback string is cached. A `ja` user on site B (default `fr`) in the same process then gets site A's German text. The same staleness happens after an admin changes `default_locale`: earlier fallback results stay cached until the process restarts.

Fallback locales are only loaded in ApplicationController, so other contexts miss fallbacks and can poison the cache

- Sidekiq jobs and mailers
- rake tasks
- controllers or middleware outside ApplicationController
- `I18n.t(..., locale: x)` calls

In those paths a key missing from the current locale falls back to locales whose translations were never loaded, so the lookup returns "translation missing: ...". For argument-less `I18n.t` calls that string is frozen into the shared LRU cache under `key+locale`. Later web requests get the cached "translation missing" text even after `ensure_loaded!` has loaded `en`.

Fix: load the fallback chain inside the patched `I18n.translate` / `load_locale`, not in a controller filter.

The PR adds a custom fallback order (user locale → site default → en), changes the loading path (`ensure_loaded!`), and turns fallbacks on in every environment, including test and development. No tests cover any of it.

There is no check that:
- a key missing in the user locale resolves from the site default locale, then from English;
- the fallback locales get loaded;
- cached translations behave correctly when the default locale changes.

Regressions such as the cache and loading issues in this change would go unnoticed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

Any stored value containing a single quote makes the migration fail with a SQL syntax error, and in general this is an injection-prone pattern. Use `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.quote(h)` or bind parameters.

The regex requires the TLD to match `[a-z]{2,5}`. This rejects many real domains such as `.museum`, `.travel`, `.digital` and `.technology`, as well as `localhost` and IP addresses. Admins cannot add these hosts through the new UI, although the previous free-form site setting accepted them. Hosts migrated via raw SQL in that format can never be edited and re-saved either.

The resulting array can contain undefined holes, so templates that iterate it (e.g. `embeddable-host` components) break. If the value is null, `obj[k].map` throws. The `hydrated || []` fallback does nothing because `map` always returns an array. Filter out missing entries and guard against non-array values.

It passes only because the Pretender handler for `/fruits/:id` always returns `fruits[0]` (apple). The `Fabricate(:embeddable_host)` in the nested before block is irrelevant. The spec gives false confidence about a host-based condition that no longer exists.

The specs for `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` and `Admin::EmbeddingController` only assert the class hierarchy. Nothing tests create/update/destroy, the defaulting of `category_id` to uncategorized, validation-error responses, or the serialized embedding payload. The bugs these specs would catch (nil handling, missing records) go undetected.

`category_id` is NOT NULL, but there is no foreign key, no validation that the category exists, and no cleanup when a category is deleted. Hosts can end up pointing at nonexistent categories: the admin UI badge is blank and imports silently go to uncategorized.

The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.

false_positives.candidate:
Public group members page now shows only the first 50 members with no way to page

The public `/groups/:name/members` page now calls `model.findMembers()`, which uses the model default `limit: 50, offset: 0`. The `group/members.hbs` template only iterates `members` and has no next/previous controls.

Previously non-automatic groups returned all members and automatic groups returned 200. Now any group with more than 50 members is silently truncated to 50 on the public page, and users cannot reach the rest.

Either add pagination or infinite loading to the public template, or keep requesting enough members there.

remove_member uses users.delete which bypasses GroupUser destroy callbacks

`group.users.delete(user_id)` on a `has_many :through` deletes the `group_users` join rows with a SQL `delete_all`. It does not destroy them, so GroupUser `after_destroy` callbacks (title/primary-group cleanup) never run. The `user_count` counter cache may also not be maintained, and this PR now displays that count and uses it for pagination.

The previous code path used `group.remove(user)`, which destroys each GroupUser and runs those callbacks. Removed users can therefore keep stale group-derived state (title, primary group), and `user_count` can drift.

- The PATCH `changes: {add:, delete:}` incremental membership API is gone.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Match statistics are written inside validation, so they get double-counted or rolled back

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count` and saves the row. It is called from `EmailValidator#validate_each`, so it runs on every validation pass. The counts end up wrong in two ways.

1. Double counting: `UsersController#create` always calls `user.valid?` (line 168; the `&&` evaluates `valid?` first) and then `user.save` (line 172), which validates again. Every signup attempt for a `do_nothing` email is counted twice.
2. Lost counts: `save`/`save!` run validations inside the record's transaction and raise `ActiveRecord::Rollback` when validation fails. When the email is actually blocked, the increment made during `save` is rolled back. Paths that only call `save!` (e.g. `User.create_for_email` for invites) never record blocked matches at all.

The result is that `match_count`/`last_match_at` are inconsistent and unreliable, which is the stated purpose of these columns. Don't write to the database from inside a validator; record the match explicitly after the create attempt, outside the user's transaction.

The candidate elaborates with concrete details (the method increments match_count and saves inside EmailValidator#validate_each, causing double-counting and rolled-back counts), which is the same underlying issue as the side effects and misleading method name described in the golden comment.

Blocked-email lookup is an exact, case-sensitive match and is trivially bypassed

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` compares the raw submitted value. Neither the stored email nor the input is downcased or stripped. If `bad@spammers.org` is blocked, a spammer can register as `Bad@spammers.org` or `BAD@SPAMMERS.ORG` and pass validation. The uniqueness validation on `BlockedEmail.email` is also case-sensitive, so case-variant duplicates can be inserted. Normalize the email (e.g. `Email.downcase(email).strip`) both when storing and when looking up, or compare with `lower(email)`.

match_count increment is a racy read-modify-write

`should_block?` loads the record, does `record.match_count += 1`, and then calls `record.save`. Concurrent signup attempts for the same email can read the same value and overwrite each other's increment, losing counts. Each save also triggers a uniqueness-validation query. Use an atomic update instead, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])`.

From then on, the inline validation for that address shows the generic `user.email.invalid` text, which is misleading for the "already taken" case. Nothing verifies that `User` actually rejects a blocked email through `valid?`/`save`. Nothing covers the new `errors`/`values` keys in the `UsersController#create` failure response that the JS now depends on, or the match-count behavior through the real controller flow. true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

include_website_name lacks `?` suffix so it is never used as an include filter

This is also why the method gives no protection for untrusted users. It should be renamed `include_website_name?`, and it should also apply the same `restrict_user_fields?` check that `website` uses.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify that include_website_name lacks the required ? suffix, preventing Rails/ActiveModel serializers from using it as a conditional include predicate. The candidate omits the string-concatenation concern but flags the same primary bug.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the TL0 untrusted-attribute restriction

For TL0 users viewed by anonymous visitors, `website` is deliberately hidden through `untrusted_attributes`, which checks `scope.restrict_user_fields?`. The new `website_name` attribute was added to the plain `attributes` list but not to `untrusted_attributes`, so it is always serialized. It contains the website host, and in the same-domain cases the full path too.

Before this change the client derived the name from `model.website`, which was absent for these users, so nothing was shown. Now `user.hbs` checks `{{#if model.website_name}}` and renders the name in a span for TL0 users.

As a result, new and untrusted (spam) accounts can again advertise their website to anonymous visitors, which is exactly what the restriction exists to prevent. Fix: add `:website_name` to `untrusted_attributes`, or make its include predicate also check `restrict_user_fields?`.

The `elsif` branch treats two hosts as the same site whenever everything after the first label matches and the instance host has more than two labels.

For instances hosted on shared domains this gives wrong results. For example, an instance at `forum.trydiscourse.com` (or `x.herokuapp.com`, `x.github.io`, `forum.co.uk`) will show the full URL path for any user website like `spam.trydiscourse.com/...` or `other.co.uk/...`. Those sites are not the instance's domain, so this contradicts the feature's intent.

The comparison is also case-sensitive: `URI#host` preserves case, so `http://Example.com/user` will not match `example.com`.

Tests don't cover website_name for TL0/anonymous or the sibling-subdomain branch

The TL0 'untrusted attributes' list does not include `website_name`, and that profile has no website set, so the spec cannot catch that `website_name` leaks for restricted users.

The new `website_name` specs only exercise the identical-host, different-host and parent-domain cases. Nothing tests the `www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com` branch, a blank website, or a website without a path. The most complex conditional in the method is effectively untested.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kernel#open on admin-supplied feed URL allows command execution / local file read

`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` relies on open-uri's patched `Kernel#open`. That only does an HTTP fetch when the string looks like a `scheme://` URL; otherwise it falls back to plain `Kernel#open`. A value like `|some shell command` runs a subprocess, and `/etc/passwd` reads a local file whose content is then imported as a public topic. The URL is never validated, so an admin (not necessarily a server operator on hosted installs) gets RCE or file disclosure. Use `URI.parse(url).open` or an HTTP client after checking the scheme is http/https.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same unvalidated open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) call. The candidate describes additional command-execution and local-file risks, but these stem from the same underlying bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring match

`discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` accepts any origin that is a prefix of `discourseUrl`. For example, `http://forum.example.co` passes when discourseUrl is `http://forum.example.com/`. A foreign origin can then send `discourse-resize` messages. Compare `e.origin` exactly against the origin parsed from `discourseUrl`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same origin-validation bug: using indexOf/substring matching allows a foreign origin that is a prefix of discourseUrl to pass, and both recommend exact origin comparison.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.

The post is then stored with `cook_method: raw_html`, so it is never sanitized. URI parsing accepts `'`, `=`, `(` and `)` in the query, so a URL such as `http:///?x'onmouseover='alert(1)` passes `TopicRetriever#invalid_host?`. Nokogiri parses the result into a real `onmouseover` attribute and keeps it in `to_html`. Anyone can trigger this by calling `/embed/best?embed_url=...` with a spoofed Referer, which leaves a script-bearing post on the forum domain. Escape the URL (e.g. `ERB::Util.html_escape`) or build the link with Nokogiri.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS vulnerability described in the golden comment: unescaped URL interpolation into raw HTML that is stored unsanitized. It provides a more detailed exploit path but addresses the same underlying bug, even though it omits the separate nil NoMethodError concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` typo turns the if/else into a modifier conditional

`end if` makes the whole if/else block a trailing `if` modifier whose condition is the next compiled ERB statement (the output-buffer append for the following text). The template only renders because that append happens to be truthy. Output is also reordered: the condition is evaluated before the block. This should be a plain `<%- end %>`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the ERB block is closed with `end if` instead of plain `end`. The candidate gives a more detailed mechanism (modifier conditional, reordered evaluation) while the golden says it will raise, but they point to the same typo and the same fix.

However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

RSS items without <content> crash the feed import

`i.content.scrub` assumes every item has a `content` element. false_positives.candidate:
raw_html cook method bypasses all HTML sanitization for imported content

When `cook_method == raw_html`, `cook` returns `raw` verbatim and skips the normal pipeline that sanitizes HTML. Imported content reaches it unfiltered from two places. The RSS job uses `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content)`, so `<script>`, `on*` handlers and `<iframe>` from the feed are stored. The Readability import whitelists `href`/`src` attributes, so `javascript:` URLs pass through. That HTML is rendered as-is in the forum and in the embed view (`raw post.cooked`). Any third-party or compromised content in the feed or blog becomes stored XSS on the Discourse origin. The imported HTML should still be run through a sanitizer/whitelist.

Unauthenticated callers can create unlimited topics by varying the embed URL

Any request with a matching Referer (trivially spoofed outside a browser) enqueues `retrieve_topic` for an arbitrary `embed_url`. The only throttle, in `TopicRetriever#retrieved_recently?`, is keyed on the exact URL string. Adding a different query string (`?a=1`, `?a=2`, ...) on the embeddable host therefore bypasses it. Each variant causes a server-side fetch and, if the host returns 200, a new topic via `import_remote`. The job is also enqueued on every hit, including the loading page's 30-second auto-reload. Consider normalizing URLs, rate limiting per IP, and limiting how many new embeds can be created.

absolutize_urls corrupts protocol-relative URLs

The checks `href.start_with?('/')` and `src.start_with?('/')` also match protocol-relative URLs like `//cdn.example.com/img.png`. `sub(/^\/+/, '')` then strips both slashes and produces `http://bloghost/cdn.example.com/img.png`. Protocol-relative image and CDN links are common in blog/RSS content, so they will be broken in imported posts. Skip values starting with `//`, or resolve properly with `URI.join(url, href)`. The same bug exists in the `img` branch at line 70.

`post = embed.post` returns nil if a moderator deleted the imported post, because Trashable's default scope hides it. When the feed content later changes, `PostRevisor.new(nil).revise!` raises NoMethodError. `PollFeed` loops over all items without rescue, so one deleted embed aborts processing of every later feed item on every hourly run. `PostCreator#create` returns the post object even when saving failed and rolled back; the post then has `errors` and `id`/`topic_id` are nil. `post.present?` is still true, so `TopicEmbed.create!(topic_id: nil, post_id: nil, ...)` runs. The throttle calls `setnx` and then `expire` in a separate command. If the process dies or Redis errors between the two calls, the key never expires and that embed URL is treated as 'retrieved recently' forever. Use a single atomic `SET key 1 NX EX 60`.

Each thread now calls `import_remote`, which fetches the link over the network. Any 404/timeout raises OpenURI::HTTPError and aborts the whole import. Non-http links make `import` return nil, so those threads are silently skipped.

`embeddable_host` is blank by default, so `ensure_embeddable` raises InvalidAccess (403) before `params.require(:embed_url)` runs. Where it hasn't, it now silently drops any existing `top_topics` table. The new `create_topic_embeds` migration uses `force: true` the same way. `t.string :embed_url` creates a varchar(255) column. Article URLs with long slugs or query strings can exceed this, and PostgreSQL then raises 'value too long' during `TopicEmbed.create!`. That fails the import job, or aborts the feed loop. Use `text`, or validate/truncate the length.
