true_positives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Loop condition and recorded filesize use `tempfile.size`, which reads a stale file descriptor after ImageOptim replaces the file

`Tempfile#size` on an open tempfile does `fstat` on its file descriptor, not on the path. `convert_with` runs `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!(to)`, and image_optim writes to a separate temp file and `rename`s it over the path. After the first iteration the path points to a new inode while `tempfile`'s descriptor still refers to the old, unlinked one.

So `tempfile.size` reports the size of the first `convert` output for every later iteration. Consequences:
- If that size is still above the limit, the loop always runs all 5 attempts and over-shrinks the image (about 0.8^5 linear) even after the real file is small enough.
- The stale size is passed as `filesize` to `Upload.create_for`, so a successfully shrunk image can still fail the max-size validation, or be stored with a wrong filesize.

Use `File.size(tempfile.path)` for both the loop check and the filesize argument, and make sure downstream code reads from the path rather than the old descriptor.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tempfile.size returns a stale cached size after the file is replaced, so the loop and downstream filesize handling use incorrect data. The candidate gives a more detailed mechanism and consequences, but it points to the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Oversized animated GIFs are silently flattened to a single frame when animated thumbnails are disabled

When `allow_animated_thumbnails` is false, `downsize_instructions` runs `convert #{from}[0] ...`, which keeps only the first frame and writes it back over the uploaded file.

Previously an oversized animated GIF got a clear "file too large" error. Now it is silently stored as a static image. Users lose their animation with no indication of why.

Consider skipping auto-downsizing for animated images that cannot be resized with animation preserved, and returning the size error instead.

Up to 5 ImageMagick + ImageOptim passes on a 10MB image run inside the web process

The new loop runs `convert` followed by a full ImageOptim pass up to 5 times on images of up to 10MB, all inside the request handling path. For API uploads with `synchronous` it runs in the request itself; otherwise it runs in `Scheduler::Defer`, a single in-process background thread shared with other deferred work.

Each iteration can take seconds of CPU on large photos, which delays all other deferred tasks in that worker. Several problems compound this:
- The `convert` exit status is ignored, so a failing conversion still costs 5 iterations.
- ImageOptim runs on every intermediate result rather than once at the end.
- The scale factor is fixed at 80% instead of being derived from the size ratio.

No tests for auto-downsizing or the changed `OptimizedImage` API

The PR changes the signature and behaviour of `OptimizedImage.downsize`/`optimize` and removes `OptimizedImage.dimensions`. It also adds a new size-reduction path in `UploadsController#create_upload`, but no specs are added or updated.

A test that calls the existing 4-argument `downsize` would have exposed the method-redefinition bug. A controller spec that uploads an image above `max_image_size_kb` would exercise the loop and filesize handling, including the stale `tempfile.size` issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError when the user has no TopicUser row

`TopicUser.find_by(user_id:, topic_id:)` returns nil when the logged-in user has never interacted with the topic. Examples: a forwarded link, a guessed URL, or the embedded-image case. The next line, `tu.notification_level`, then raises and the request returns a 500. Use `TopicUser.change`, which creates the row if missing, or handle nil explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: TopicUser.find_by returns nil when no record exists, and calling notification_level on it crashes. The candidate describes the same nil-handling failure with equivalent wording.

false_positives.candidate:
State-changing unsubscribe exposed over GET (CSRF / embedded-image muting)

`unsubscribe` changes the user's notification level, but it is routed as a plain GET (`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"`) with no token or confirmation, and `check_xhr` is skipped. Any page or forum post the logged-in user's browser loads can trigger it, for example a post containing `![](/t/foo/123/unsubscribe)`. Every viewer is then silently demoted on topic 123, and after a second load they are muted. The `TopicUser` update runs before `respond_to`, so it is saved even when the request is an image fetch. Existing mutations such as `mute`/`unmute`/`set_notifications` use PUT/POST. Fix: make the mutation a POST from the Ember page, or require a signed per-user key in the URL.

Direct `tu.save!` bypasses TopicUser.change, so the unsubscribe can be silently reverted

Assigning `notification_level` and calling `save!` skips what `TopicUser.change` does: setting `notifications_reason_id = user_changed` and `notifications_changed_at`, and publishing the MessageBus `notification_level_change`.

Users who were auto-tracked through `update_last_read` have `notifications_reason_id` NULL. For them, both `update_last_read` (`case when tu.notifications_reason_id is null and ... then :tracking`) and `TopicUser.auto_track` will bump the level back to tracking on the next read or post, undoing the unsubscribe.

Other open tabs also never learn about the change because nothing is published on MessageBus. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic_id, notification_level: ...)`.

Toggle logic does not stop the emails it promises to stop, and repeat visits escalate to muted

If the level is above regular it drops only to regular; otherwise it mutes.

Reply, mention and quote emails are also sent at the regular level. A tracking user who clicks the link in a 'replied' email ends up at regular and keeps receiving exactly those emails. Meanwhile the page tells them 'You will stop receiving notifications for <title>'.

The action is also not idempotent. Refreshing the page, a browser prefetch, or clicking a second email link moves the user one more step down, from regular to muted. The intended target level should be explicit, for example always muted, or at least below the level that triggers the email type that was clicked.

Explicit `render :show` happens before `show` sets canonical_url, dropping the topic canonical link

`perform_show_response` now calls `render :show` inside `format.html`. Rails renders the template and layout immediately at that call.

In `show`, `canonical_url UrlHelper.absolute_without_cdn(...)` runs afterwards (line 87). Previously the implicit render happened at the end of the action, so `@canonical_url` was already set. Now the layout's canonical link tag is rendered without it and falls back to the request path. Post-number URLs like `/t/slug/123/45` then advertise themselves as canonical, which is an SEO and duplicate-content regression. Move the `canonical_url` call before `perform_show_response`, or set it inside it.

Client-side transition to the unsubscribe route shows the confirmation without unsubscribing

The route's model hook calls `PostStream.loadTopicView(params.id)`. That uses the preloaded `topic_<id>` payload, or otherwise fetches `/t/<id>.json`; it never hits `/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe`.

Only a full page load reaches `TopicsController#unsubscribe`. If the user reaches this route through in-app navigation, or once the preload has been consumed, the page claims 'You will stop receiving notifications' but no server-side change is made.

Logged-out users clicking the email link lose the unsubscribe intent

`unsubscribe` was added to `ensure_logged_in`. Many recipients click email links on a device where they are not logged in. For a non-XHR GET, the NotLoggedIn handling sends them to the homepage, with no return-to path and no message. The unsubscribe silently does not happen, and the user has no indication they need to log in and retry.

add_unsubscribe_link now implicitly requires unsubscribe_url

The `unsubscribe_link` translation now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}`. Any caller (core or plugin) that passes `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without `unsubscribe_url` will hit `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` in both `body` (line 90) and `html_part`. The spec had to be changed to pass a dummy URL for this reason.

The text 'stop receiving notifications about this particular topic' also only makes sense for topic emails. Consider a separate translation key, appended only when `unsubscribe_url` is present.

No tests for the new unsubscribe endpoint or for the per-topic link in emails

The only spec change passes a dummy `unsubscribe_url` so the existing test does not crash. Nothing asserts that the URL actually appears in the body or HTML part.

There are no controller specs for `TopicsController#unsubscribe`, covering:
- the level transitions (watching/tracking to regular, regular to muted),
- the slug redirect,
- the missing-TopicUser case,
- the logged-out case.

Those are where the bugs above live.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateMany with empty data is a no-op, so SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is never bumped

`SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` passes an empty `data` object. Prisma only fills in `@updatedAt` when there are other fields to write. With no write arguments the query engine skips the UPDATE, so `updatedAt` on SelectedCalendar is never refreshed. The stated purpose ("Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars under this credential") is not achieved. The call still adds a DB round-trip on every webhook-driven cache refresh. Either set `updatedAt: new Date()` explicitly or remove the call; the PR notes already say the frontend doesn't use this field.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: calling updateManyByCredentialId with an empty data object does not trigger Prisma's @updatedAt behavior, so SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is not refreshed. The candidate's explicit updatedAt fix matches the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`sed -i ''` is macOS-only; script fails on Linux and exits 0 on errors

`sed -i '' -E ...` is BSD sed syntax. On GNU sed, `''` is parsed as the (empty) script and the substitution expression as a filename, so updating an existing `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` fails on Linux. `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved relative to the caller's cwd rather than the script location. `cleanup` always does `exit 0`, so rate-limit and URL-extraction failures report success.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same bug: `sed -i ''` uses macOS/BSD syntax and fails on Linux/GNU sed. Additional concerns do not change the core match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization failure thrown as plain Error, surfaces as 500

When the credential doesn't belong to the user, the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. tRPC maps plain errors to INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR. A legitimate not-found/forbidden case is therefore reported and logged as a server crash, and the client can't tell the two apart. Throw a `TRPCError` with code `NOT_FOUND` or `FORBIDDEN` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: authentication/authorization failures are thrown as plain Error objects, which tRPC maps to a 500/INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR. Both recommend throwing a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code such as FORBIDDEN (candidate also allows NOT_FOUND).

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp formatted with hardcoded en-US locale

`new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` ignores the user's locale and time format preference (12h/24h). Non-US users see a US-style date like 7/15/25, 4:06 PM inside an otherwise translated string. Use the locale from `useLocale()` (i18n.language) or the app's existing date formatting helpers.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: date formatting uses a hardcoded 'en-US' locale rather than the user's locale from useLocale, causing incorrect date representation for non-US users.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting the cache doesn't invalidate connectedCalendars, so the UI keeps showing stale cache status

`deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` prop. It never invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. In contrast, `disconnectMutation` invalidates it in `onSettled`. On pages where `onChanged` isn't provided (e.g. /apps/installed/calendar), and because the query uses `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`, the dropdown keeps showing "Cache Status / Last updated …" and the "Delete cached data" action after a successful deletion. Users get no feedback that the cache is gone. Add an `onSettled` that invalidates `connectedCalendars`.

Backfilled updatedAt = migration time makes existing caches appear freshly updated

`ADD COLUMN "updatedAt" ... DEFAULT NOW()` stamps every existing CalendarCache row with the migration timestamp. The new UI shows "Last updated: <timestamp>" from this column. Right after deploy, every user with an existing cache will see it as freshly updated, even if the data is up to a month old (CACHING_TIME). That is misleading in a feature meant to show cache freshness. A better backfill would be something like `expiresAt - interval '30 days'`.

Migration warning comment contradicts the SQL

The auto-generated header says the column is added "without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty." The statement below does add `DEFAULT NOW()`, so the warning is false and will confuse anyone auditing migrations. Remove or correct it.

Cache status counts expired entries that are never served

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups over all CalendarCache rows for the credential with no `expiresAt >= now` filter. `getCachedAvailability` only returns non-expired rows. A credential whose cache has fully expired, and is therefore never used, will still show a cache status and a "Last updated" timestamp in the UI. Filter on `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` so the status reflects cache that is actually in effect.

Handler bypasses calendar-cache feature gating by instantiating the real repository directly

The handler does `new CalendarCacheRepository()` directly instead of going through `CalendarCache.init`, which selects `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` when the feature is disabled. As a result, the mock's new `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` is never used. Users whose team has calendar-cache disabled, but who still have leftover rows, will see cache status and delete actions. The handler also adds an unconditional groupBy query to every connectedCalendars request.

UserWithCalendars now requires unused updatedAt/googleChannelId fields

The `Pick` for `allSelectedCalendars` and `userLevelSelectedCalendars` now requires `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId`. Neither field is read anywhere in this module. The type is part of the public `getConnectedDestinationCalendars` export (legacy export for @calcom/platform-libraries), so every caller must now select these columns or fail type-checking. To satisfy it, `findUnlockedUserForSession` in user.ts now loads these columns for every session. Revert the type widening unless something actually consumes the fields.

dev:cron depends on undeclared tsx via npx

`dev:cron` now runs `npx tsx`, but `tsx` isn't a declared dependency while `ts-node` still is. npx will download an unpinned tsx at runtime, or fail offline. The change is also unrelated to this feature. Add `tsx` as a devDependency or keep ts-node.

No tests for new deleteCache authorization or cache status query

The PR adds a mutation that deletes data scoped by an ownership check, plus a new groupBy repository method. There are no unit or integration tests for either. Cases worth covering: deleting another user's credential cache must be rejected, and `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` must return the max `updatedAt` per credential. The PR description itself notes end-to-end testing was not possible.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Slot end used for the working-hours check is computed from the slot start

`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is identical to `start`. The intended `end > workingHour.endTime` check therefore only tests the slot's start.

A slot that starts inside working hours but runs past their end is accepted. For example, a 60-minute event at 17:30 with working hours ending at 18:00 passes. This should use `slotEndTime`, taking care with slots that end exactly at midnight.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: the slot end is computed from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, so the working-hours check only validates the start and accepts slots that extend past the end.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with `===`, so the 'unavailable all day' branch never runs

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two freshly created object references, so it is always false. Overrides that mark a day unavailable (start == end) never take this early-reject path.

The later checks miss a slot starting exactly at the override instant (midnight in the organizer's zone), because `slotStartTime.isAfter(end)` is false for equal times. Since `dateOverrideExist` is then true, the function returns true and also skips the busy check. A slot at midnight on a day the host marked unavailable can therefore be offered. Use `.isSame(...)` or compare `valueOf()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: dayjs objects compared with === are distinct references, so the check is always false and the unavailable-all-day path never runs. The candidate's extra downstream impact detail and alternative valueOf() fix do not change the core issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Slots on a date-override day skip the busy-time check, allowing double bookings

When the slot's day has a date override and the slot passes the range checks, `checkIfIsAvailable` hits `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;`. That returns before `busy.every(...)` runs.

On any day with a date override, the user's existing Cal bookings and connected-calendar busy times are therefore ignored. All users of a non-team event count as fixed hosts, so this affects personal event types too, not only round-robin. Invitees can book slots that overlap existing bookings or calendar events.

Only the working-hours check should be skipped when an override exists. The busy check must still run.

Working-hours check rejects every slot when a user has more than one working-hours entry for a day

`workingHours.find(...)` returns true, and the slot is rejected, if the slot falls outside ANY working-hours entry that includes the slot's UTC weekday. It should only reject when the slot is inside none of them.

`getWorkingHours` splits ranges that cross UTC midnight into two entries with shifted `days`. Example: a PST user working Mon–Fri 9–17 gets {days 1–5, 1020–1439} and {days 2–6, 0–60}.
- A Tuesday 18:00Z slot fits the first entry but is outside the second, so it is rejected.
- A Tuesday 00:30Z slot is rejected by the first entry.

Result: organizers in most western-hemisphere timezones lose almost all Tue–Fri availability. Users with split schedules (e.g. 9–12 and 13–17 on the same day) lose all slots on those days.

The logic should accept a slot that fits within at least one applicable entry.

Multiple date-override ranges on the same day reject all slots

`dateOverrides.find` returns true, and the slot is marked unavailable, as soon as ANY override on the slot's day doesn't contain the slot.

Date overrides support several time ranges per day (e.g. 9–10 and 14–15). A slot in the first range is outside the second, and vice versa, so every slot on that day is rejected for the fixed host. The check should reject only when the slot is outside ALL override ranges for that day.

Override day is matched by UTC calendar day instead of the organizer's local day, and formatted in server-local time

The code checks whether the slot is on the override's day by comparing the UTC date of the override's real start instant with the slot's UTC date. A date override covers a calendar day in the organizer's timezone.

Example: a PST organizer sets an override for day D 16:00–20:00, i.e. D+1 00:00Z–04:00Z. The real start falls on UTC day D+1.
- Slots during the organizer's day D (e.g. D 17:00Z = 09:00 PST) don't match, so normal working hours apply and they are wrongly offered.
- Slots on UTC day D+1 (a normal day for the organizer) match and are wrongly rejected as outside the override.

Separately, `dayjs(date.start).add(...).format(...)` formats in the server's local timezone, while `slotStartTime` is in UTC. The comparison also breaks on any server not running in UTC.

The slot should be converted to `organizerTimeZone` and its local date compared with the override's date.

Timezone-shifted overrides that cross invitee midnight are silently dropped

The shifted start/end are reduced to `hour()*60 + minute()`, which discards the day.

If shifting by `inviteeOffset - organizerOffset` pushes the override across the invitee's midnight, `endTime` wraps below `startTime`. Example: a UTC override 16:00–22:00 for an IST invitee becomes 21:30 → 1290 and 03:30 → 210.

`buildSlots` skips any boundary with `start >= end`, so the whole override vanishes. The user's working hours for that day have already been removed, so the invitee sees no slots at all from that host. The range needs to be split at midnight, or clamped to the invitee's day.

Active-override day selection still uses the naive organizer wall time, so the new offset is applied to the wrong invitee day

`override.start` holds the organizer's wall-clock time stored as UTC. The filter `dayjs.utc(override.start).isBetween(startOfInviteeDay, ...)` compares that naive value with real instants of the invitee's day, without converting it.

Example: an IST override on D 15:00–18:00 (real D 09:30Z = 19:30 Brisbane on D). For a Brisbane (+10) invitee the naive D T15:00Z falls in invitee day D+1.
- The shifted 19:30–22:30 window is shown on D+1.
- The host's normal working hours are removed on D+1.
- Day D keeps the normal working hours.

The PR's timezone fix is incomplete without converting `override.start` to a real instant, using `override.timeZone`, before this day filter.

Missing override timeZone silently falls back to the server's local timezone

`TimeRange.timeZone` is optional. When it is undefined, `dayjs(...).tz(override.timeZone)` resolves to the process's local zone rather than UTC.

Any caller of `getSlots` that passes overrides without `timeZone` now gets them shifted by `inviteeOffset - serverLocalOffset`. Previously they were used as-is, so results now depend on the server or client machine timezone. Either require `timeZone` or skip the shift when it is absent.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount delete branch is not scoped to SMS and cannot use the existing index

The `deleteMany` OR has a second branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` with no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter. The SMS cron will therefore delete EMAIL or WHATSAPP reminders with `retryCount > 1`. Today only this handler increments the counter, but any other reminder cron that adopts the new column would have its reminders deleted by the SMS cron, which is surprising cross-method data loss.

The branch is also unindexed. `retryCount` has no index, and the OR stops Postgres from relying on `@@index([method, scheduled, scheduledDate])`. This is likely to become a sequential scan of the whole WorkflowReminder table (all methods, all history) on every cron run.

Fix: add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and probably `scheduled: false`) to the second branch.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core bug: the deleteMany OR branch on retryCount > 1 lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, so the SMS cron deletes non-SMS reminders (EMAIL/WHATSAPP). The extra indexing note does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Transient failures permanently delete reminders after two cron runs

The catch block increments `retryCount` for any exception in the try body. That includes transient errors such as Twilio 5xx or 429 rate limits, network timeouts, the `prisma.profile.findFirst` or `getBookerBaseUrl` calls, and template rendering. It also includes the `scheduled: true` update failing after Twilio already accepted the message.

After two failures the row is deleted on the next run. Previously the reminder would be retried until its scheduled date (up to 7 days out). Now a short Twilio or DB outage spanning two cron invocations silently and permanently drops every SMS reminder processed during it.

If the post-schedule update is what failed, the reminder is retried and deleted while a Twilio message is already queued. That causes duplicate sends, and the `referenceId` needed to cancel the queued message is lost.

Only known-permanent errors (e.g. Twilio invalid-number error codes) should count toward deletion, or the retry budget should be larger or time-based.

SMS-locked users/teams have their reminders deleted

`twilio.scheduleSMS` returns `undefined`, not an error, when the user or team has `smsLockState === LOCKED`. This new `else` branch treats that as a failed attempt and increments `retryCount`, so after two cron runs every pending SMS reminder for that account is deleted.

Previously these reminders stayed unscheduled and would be sent if an admin unlocked the account, for example after a false-positive abuse lock. Now unlocking does not restore them and attendees silently get no reminders.

The locked case should be distinguished from a real scheduling failure.

Failure inside the catch handler aborts the whole cron run

The catch block now awaits `prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` before logging. If that update throws, the exception escapes the `for` loop and the handler. This happens for example when the original error was a DB connectivity problem, or when the row was deleted concurrently (e.g. a booking cancellation), which makes Prisma throw `P2025`.

All remaining reminders in the batch are then skipped, the endpoint returns 500, and the original error is never logged. Before this PR the catch only logged, so one bad reminder could not stop the rest.

Wrap the counter update in its own try/catch, or log first and ignore update failures.

Reminders with no recipient or empty message are still retried indefinitely

The PR's goal is to stop endlessly re-processing reminders that can never be sent. However, when `sendTo` is null (e.g. `smsReminderNumber` missing) or the rendered message is empty, the `if` at this line is skipped. Neither branch increments `retryCount`, so these reminders are still re-fetched and fully re-processed on every cron run until their scheduled date. That includes the profile lookup, booker-URL resolution and template rendering. These permanently unsendable cases are arguably the ones that most need the retry cap.

No tests for the new retry/deletion behavior

The PR adds behavior that deletes user-facing reminders, but no tests cover it. Cases worth testing: incrementing `retryCount` on a falsy `scheduleSMS` result and on thrown errors, deleting reminders with `retryCount > 1`, leaving reminders of other methods untouched, and not deleting on success. Given the data-loss risk if the conditions are wrong, these should be covered.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

true_positives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unreachable branches in getBaseConditions

`getAuthorizationConditions()` always returns a `Prisma.Sql` object, which is always truthy. Even the NOTHING case is a non-null Sql instance.

As a result, the `else if (filterConditions)` branch and the final `else return NOTHING_CONDITION` can never run. This is harmless today, but it suggests a fallback that does not exist.

If auth were ever made nullable, the `filterConditions`-only branch would silently drop authorization. Simplify to `filterConditions ? (auth) AND (filter) : auth`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unreachable-branch issue in getBaseConditions: getAuthorizationConditions always returns a truthy Prisma.Sql, so the filterConditions-only and final else branches can never execute.

false_positives.candidate:
Top-level OR fragments are returned without outer parentheses, so composing them gives wrong results

`Prisma.sql` inlines nested fragments verbatim; it does not wrap them in parentheses. Several public methods return a fragment whose top level is an unparenthesized OR:
- `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` / `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` return `(A AND B) OR (C AND D)`.
- `buildFilterConditions` returns `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` when only one filter is set.
- `getBaseConditions` returns the auth fragment bare when there are no filters.

These methods are the replacement for `findMany`, so callers must embed the fragments in their own queries. A natural pattern is `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "createdAt" >= ${start}`. That parses as `(team branch) OR ((user branch) AND createdAt >= start)`, so date, status or any other extra predicate applies to only one branch. The result is wrong counts and leaked rows outside the requested range.

Placeholder "refresh_token" overwrites the real refresh token in the default path

The fallback `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` also runs when sync is disabled. Office365's `refreshTokenResponseSchema` makes `refresh_token` optional, and the caller spreads `tokenResponse.data` over the stored credentials. Previously, if Microsoft omitted a refresh_token, the existing one was kept. Now it is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token", and every later refresh fails permanently. Only inject the placeholder in sync mode, or don't inject it at all.

appStoreMetadata is indexed by slug, but it is keyed by app directory name

`appStoreMetadata` is generated keyed by app directory name (e.g. `googlecalendar`, `zoomvideo`, `office365calendar`), not by slug. Looking it up with `app.slug` (`google-calendar`, `zoom`, `office365-calendar`, `msteams`) returns undefined, so the webhook answers 404 for most of the OAuth apps this PR targets. It only works by accident where slug equals dirName. Select `dirName` from the App row and index by that.

`prisma` used without being imported

The new `prisma.credential.update(...)` call references `prisma`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. At best it resolves to the dev-only `globalThis.prisma`. In production that global is not set, so this throws a ReferenceError/TypeError. Since `getClient` runs in the constructor, every Salesforce booking/CRM operation fails.

Zoom sends app slug "zoomvideo" instead of "zoom"

Zoom's app slug and appId is "zoom" (see `createOAuthAppCredential({ appId: "zoom" ...})` in the callback). The webhook also identifies apps by slug. The refresh call sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, the directory name, so the self-hoster's sync endpoint gets an identifier that doesn't match what it uses for the webhook. Zoom refreshes will fail or return the wrong app's tokens.

Webex, Lark and MS Teams still require the provider-native response shape in sync mode

Webex validates the response with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` directly, which requires a scope literal, token_type, refresh_token and refresh_token_expires_in. Lark runs it through `handleLarkError`, which expects `{code:0,data:{...}}`. MS Teams overwrites the entire stored key with the response. All three are routed to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, whose documented contract is "only the access token and expiry date". With a conforming endpoint, Webex rejects every refresh, Lark throws, and Teams loses its refresh_token. The endpoint contract is not consistent across the integrations this PR switches over.

Outbound sync request carries no authentication

Cal.com POSTs only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` to the sync endpoint, with no shared secret, signature or encryption. The inbound webhook, by contrast, requires a secret and AES-encrypted keys. The self-hoster's endpoint therefore has no way to verify that the caller is Cal.com. Anyone who can reach it can enumerate user ids and obtain live third-party access tokens. Send the webhook secret or an HMAC header, and ideally encrypt the response with the shared key. Also check `response.ok` before returning.

The secret is compared with `!==`, which leaks timing information. If the header is sent more than once it becomes a `string[]` and never matches. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on the buffers after checking the lengths. The endpoint also accepts any HTTP method.

The old code logged the zod error and the raw Microsoft response when parsing failed. Now `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws a generic "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" and the MS error body is lost. That makes Outlook token problems much harder to debug. The behavior also changed from "keep the old token and continue" to "throw".

The PR changes token refresh for about ten integrations and adds a credential-writing webhook, and it states that no tests were added or run. Unit tests for `parseRefreshTokenResponse` would have caught several of the issues above: the returned wrapper object, the fields stripped by the broken schema, and the placeholder refresh_token. That is the exact behaviour the PR identifies as broken: it consumes SendGrid's 100 pending-cancellation quota, and once the quota is full these cancels fail and rescheduled-booking reminders are still sent.

The `immediateDelete` branch in `emailReminderManager.ts` also returns without deleting the row or marking it cancelled. The row stays with `scheduled: true` and its `referenceId`. If it was already `cancelled: true` (from `requestReschedule`), or is later marked cancelled by a workflow edit, the cron sends a second cancel for the same batch.

One failed SendGrid cancel aborts the whole cancellation batch on every cron run

One `try` wraps the entire `for` loop of `client.request` calls, and the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` promises run only at the end via `Promise.all`. Prisma promises are lazy, so if any cancel request throws, the loop stops and none of the queued deletes execute.

This includes reminders that SendGrid already cancelled earlier in the same run. They keep `cancelled: true`, so the next run re-POSTs a cancel for those batch ids. SendGrid can reject a cancel for a batch that is already cancelled, and that failure aborts the loop again.

Concrete triggers:
- the 100 pending-cancellation limit;
- a batch already cancelled through the `immediateDelete` path (e.g. organizer `requestReschedule` sets `cancelled=true`, then the attendee reschedules and `handleNewBooking` cancels the same batch immediately);

One bad row therefore blocks every other cancellation until its `scheduledDate` passes, and those other emails are sent. Handle each reminder in its own try/catch and delete or mark each row right after its own request succeeds.

A workflow active on many event types can easily have more than 100 scheduled reminders in the 72h window. Past the account-wide limit, the remaining cancels fail. The failures are only logged inside `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`, and the rows are then cascade-deleted with the workflow or step, so nothing retries. Those reminders are still delivered after the user deleted the workflow.

This path needs its own deferred mechanism, for example detaching or keeping cancelled rows instead of cascade-deleting them before the cron processes them.

Every cancellation with a `referenceId` is now deferred to the cron by setting `cancelled: true`, whatever the reminder's `scheduledDate`. The cron runs every 15 minutes, and SendGrid only honours a scheduled-send cancel made at least ~10 minutes before send time.

If a booking is cancelled or rescheduled roughly 10–25 minutes before its reminder is due, the cron may not run before the cutoff, so the email goes out. The previous immediate cancel would have stopped it.

This will trip lint (no-unused-vars) and formatting checks.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Non-atomic read-modify-write lets a backup code be reused and can resurrect consumed codes

The code consumes a backup code by:
1. reading `user.backupCodes`,
2. decrypting and finding the index in memory,
3. writing back the re-encrypted array.

There is no transaction, optimistic version check or conditional update.

Two concurrent login requests with the same code will both pass validation and both succeed, which breaks the documented "each backup code can be used exactly once" guarantee. Two concurrent logins with *different* codes will each write their own snapshot. The later write overwrites the earlier one, so a consumed code becomes valid again (lost update).

Use an atomic conditional update (e.g. `updateMany` where `backupCodes` equals the value read, retrying on 0 rows) or a row lock inside a transaction.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying concurrency bug: non-atomic read-modify-write of backupCodes allows two concurrent logins with the same code to both pass validation and succeed, violating one-time-use semantics. The extra lost-update scenario is additional detail, not a different issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup-code login skips password verification when any totpCode is also sent

The password is only checked when `user.password && !credentials.totpCode` (line 121). The new backup-code branch is evaluated before the TOTP branch and only needs `credentials.backupCode` to be truthy.

An attacker can POST to the credentials callback with `email`, any `password`, any non-empty `totpCode` (e.g. "1") and a valid `backupCode`. Because a totpCode is present, the password check is skipped. The backup-code branch then accepts the request without ever looking at the TOTP value.

The result is that a single leaked backup code plus the user's email is enough to take over the account. The codes are typically saved in the downloaded `cal-backup-codes.txt` or on the clipboard. This defeats the purpose of a *second* factor.

Fix: always verify the password when a backup code is used, or check the password based on identity provider rather than on whether `totpCode` is present.

Dismissing the backup-codes step via ESC/overlay leaves UI showing 2FA as disabled

After a successful `enable` call, the modal now switches to `DisplayBackupCodes` instead of calling `onEnable()`. `onEnable` is only invoked from the "Close" button.

If the user dismisses the dialog with ESC or by clicking outside, `onOpenChange` fires instead. The parent just toggles `open`, so its `enabled` state is never set and `viewer.me` is never invalidated. The settings switch therefore shows 2FA as off even though it is enabled server-side.

The component's `step` state also stays at `DisplayBackupCodes`. Clicking the switch again reopens the modal on the backup-codes screen instead of the enable flow.

Call `onEnable` (or equivalent state sync) when the modal is closed from this step, or handle it in `onOpenChange`.

Copy button reports success unconditionally and crashes when Clipboard API is unavailable

The result of `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` is neither awaited nor caught, and the success toast is shown immediately. If the write is rejected (for example, no permission), the user is told the codes were copied when they were not, and they may close the only screen that ever shows the codes.

On self-hosted instances served over plain HTTP (non-localhost), `navigator.clipboard` is `undefined`. The handler then throws a TypeError and nothing is copied.

Await the promise and show an error toast on failure.

"missing_backup_codes" tells users to generate codes in settings, but no such feature exists

The message reads "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." This PR adds no way to generate or regenerate backup codes. They are only created in `setup.ts`, which refuses to run when 2FA is already enabled.

This matters in two cases:
- Users who enabled 2FA before this migration have `backupCodes = null`. They get this message and cannot follow it except by disabling and re-enabling 2FA.
- Users who exhaust all 10 codes have an array of `null`s. They get `incorrect_backup_code` rather than any guidance.

Either add a regenerate flow or reword the message to the actual remedy.

tabIndex=-1 on shared PasswordField toggle removes keyboard access to show/hide password

Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the visibility toggle button in the shared `PasswordField` makes the show/hide control unreachable by keyboard. This applies to every password field in the app, not just the 2FA modals.

This is an accessibility regression for keyboard and screen-reader users, and it is unrelated to the backup-code feature.

Backup codes stored reversibly encrypted rather than hashed

Backup codes are only ever compared for equality and never need to be shown again after setup. Even so, they are stored with `symmetricEncrypt` using the app-wide `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.

Anyone who obtains a DB dump plus that key can recover every user's unused backup codes in plaintext. Hashing each code (as is done for passwords) would avoid this. The TOTP secret has to be reversible, but backup codes do not.

No tests for logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code; enable test asserts nothing

The new authentication paths have no tests:
- backup-code login in `next-auth-options.ts`;
- backup-code disable in `disable.ts`;
- one-time consumption of a code.

The PR leaves a TODO for these instead.

In the first test, `expect(page.locator(...).isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` passes a Promise to `expect`, so it always passes, as the added FIXME admits. The test also navigates to logout without waiting for the enable request or the new backup-codes screen, so it can race.

The copy test only waits for the toast, which is shown regardless of whether the clipboard write succeeded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TypeError when Google Meet is the location and there is no destination calendar

`const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` yields `undefined` when `destinationCalendar` is null or `[]`. Many callers in this PR now pass `[]`, and handleNewBooking passes `null`. The next line reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. Any booking whose location is Google Meet and whose user has no destination calendar now throws inside `EventManager.create`. Previously this case fell back to Cal Video. Use `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: destructuring evt.destinationCalendar when it is null or empty makes mainHostDestinationCalendar undefined, leading to an unsafe access of its integration property.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google deleteEvent fallback is dead code; events in non-primary calendars aren't deleted

The same impossible `find(cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` is used when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it always falls through to "primary". If the event lives in a non-primary destination calendar, Google returns 404. The code resolves 404 silently, so the cancelled booking's event stays on the user's calendar.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same impossible calendar lookup condition (`externalId === externalCalendarId`), which can never match the intended calendar. The candidate describes a specific deleteEvent fallback consequence of that bug, but the underlying logic error is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Organization slug logic inverted

The original code was `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })`, which sets the slug directly only when billing is disabled. The new code is `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, which inverts it. Without team billing (for example, self-hosted), organizations are now created with no slug at all. With billing enabled, the slug is claimed immediately alongside `requestedSlug`, bypassing the payment flow. This unrelated change should be reverted.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same inverted conditional around IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED: slug is now set when billing is enabled instead of disabled, so billing-enabled orgs get both slug and requestedSlug while disabled orgs get neither.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing credential for one host's reference makes the whole reschedule throw

When a reference's credential is in neither `this.calendarCredentials` nor the DB (for example, a team member removed their calendar app), `credential` is `undefined`. It is still passed to `updateEvent`, which dereferences `credential.appName` and rejects. `return Promise.all(result)` is not awaited inside the `try`, so the `catch` never sees the rejection and the whole reschedule fails. Now that every host's reference is processed, this is much easier to hit. Skip references without a resolved credential.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: a reference with a credentialId whose credential is missing leaves credential undefined, which is passed to updateEvent and causes a runtime failure. The candidate adds details about Promise.all rejection handling, but the underlying issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Video booking references no longer store credentialId

Before: `credentialId: isCalendarType ? evt.destinationCalendar?.credentialId : result.credentialId`. After: `credentialId: isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`. Video results from `createMeeting` carry a `credentialId`, which is now dropped. handleCancelBooking only deletes a video meeting when `bookingVideoReference.credentialId` is set. As a result, Zoom/Teams/etc. meetings for new bookings are orphaned on cancellation. Keep `result.credentialId` for non-calendar results too.

Destinations without credentialId: externalCalendarId lost and team members' calendars resolved against the organizer's credentials

For a destination with no `credentialId` (legacy rows), the code calls `createEvent(c, event)` without `destination.externalId`. The resulting reference therefore stores no `externalCalendarId`; previously it stored `evt.destinationCalendar.externalId`. Later updates and deletes then can't target the right calendar.

The credentials are also taken from `this.calendarCredentials`, which holds only the organizer's credentials. If a collective team member's destination calendar lacks a credentialId, an extra event is created in every organizer calendar of that integration type. The organizer gets duplicates and the team member gets nothing.

updateLocation references lose externalCalendarId and credentialId

The references now use `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`. For calendar results these come from `CalendarManager.updateEvent`, which returns neither field. editLocation persists these as new booking references with null `externalCalendarId` and `credentialId`. Previously both fell back to `evt.destinationCalendar`. Later cancellation or reschedule then falls into the legacy path or targets the wrong calendar.

Rescheduling with newBookingId deletes only the first old calendar event

The update loop now handles one calendar reference per host. The old-event cleanup still uses `booking.references.find(...)`, so it deletes only the first old calendar reference. For collective bookings, every other host keeps a stale event at the old time in their calendar.

Error message built but no longer logged in updateAllCalendarEvents

`console.error(message)` was removed. `message` is still computed and then unused. Failures updating calendar events are now swallowed silently and only appear as generic `success: false` results, which makes production issues hard to diagnose.

Google createEvent ignores destination calendars without credentialId

The calendar is now chosen only by `cal.credentialId === credentialId`, with fallback to "primary". Legacy destination calendars with a null `credentialId` used to have their `externalId` respected. They now silently get events written to the primary calendar instead of the user's configured destination calendar.

Hangout-link patch uses a possibly undefined calendarId

`selectedCalendar` used to be guaranteed to be a string (`"primary"` fallback). It is now `undefined` whenever no destination matches the credential, and only the insert call applies `|| "primary"`. The follow-up `calendar.events.patch({ calendarId: selectedCalendar, ... })` then gets `undefined` and fails, so the Meet link is never written into the description. The patch promise is not awaited or caught, so the failure is an unhandled rejection.

Non-Google services always use the main host's calendar id, so multi-host only works for Google

EventManager calls `createEvent` once per host's credential, but Office365 (and Lark in the same way) always uses `destinationCalendar[0].externalId`, the main host's calendar. For a second host with Outlook, the request goes to `/me/calendars/<main host calendar id>/events` with the second host's token and fails. The PR's stated goal that every host with any calendar app gets the event is not met for these providers. Pick the destination matching the credential, as the Google service does.

CalDAV createEvent silently creates nothing for secondary hosts

The calendars are filtered by the main host's destination `externalId`. A secondary host's CalDAV account never contains that URL, so the filter yields zero calendars. `Promise.all([])` succeeds, and `createEvent` returns success with a uid. A booking reference is stored for an event that was never created, and the host gets nothing in their calendar.

Collective hosts' calendars are dropped when the organizer has no destination calendar

`evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` then does nothing, so every other host's destination calendar is discarded. Initialize to `[]`, or assign `teamDestinationCalendars` when the value is null.

Unrelated loadUsers rewrite drops organization select and changes error semantics

The dynamic-user query no longer selects `organization: { slug }`, so dynamic group bookings lose the organizer's org data that was previously loaded. The rewrite also turns an empty or invalid `dynamicUserList` into a generic 500 "Unable to load users" and re-wraps any HttpError as 400, discarding its original status code. These behavior changes are outside the PR's scope and untested.

Recurring cancellation repeats per reference and misses other hosts' events

The recurring-series deletion block now sits inside the `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With N calendar references it runs N times. Each run iterates all organizer credentials and deletes the first calendar reference of each updated booking, sending redundant API calls. It still uses only the organizer's credentials and only the first reference per booking. For collective recurring bookings, the other hosts' events are never deleted.

Confirmation and payment flows build evt with only one destination calendar

Only handleNewBooking adds the collective hosts' destination calendars. Paths that create calendar events later rebuild `evt` with only the booking's or organizer's destination calendar: confirm.handler → handleConfirmation, and the Stripe/PayPal webhooks → `EventManager.create`. Collective events that require confirmation or payment still create the event only on the main host's calendar, so issue #7754 remains for those flows.

Webhook payload `destinationCalendar` changes from object to array (breaking)

`CalendarEvent` is spread directly into webhook payloads (BOOKING_CREATED, CANCELLED, REJECTED, etc.). `destinationCalendar` changes from an object or null to an array. It is also inconsistent across triggers: `null` from handleNewBooking but `[]` from other paths, as the e2e test now expects. This breaks third-party webhook consumers, contradicting the PR's 'non-breaking' claim, and needs a migration note or payload compatibility shim.

Multi-destination create/update/delete paths have no tests

The PR changes `CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar` to an array and rewrites `createAllCalendarEvents`, `updateAllCalendarEvents` and the cancel-booking deletion loop to iterate multiple references and credentials. The PR states no tests were added. The regressions above (Meet crash on empty array, dead fallback lookups, dropped credentialId on references) would be caught by basic unit tests of these paths.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
requestReschedule fires async forEach without awaiting; getCalendar failures become unhandled rejections

`requestReschedule` now uses `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })`. Because the promises are discarded, the mutation goes on to send emails and webhooks and then resolves without knowing whether any calendar or video event was deleted.

Any rejection from `getCalendar` (for example a CalendarService constructor failing to parse or decrypt the key) or from `deleteEvent` / `deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled promise rejection. It does not become a tRPC error.

Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))`, optionally with per-item `.catch` and logging.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments address the same failure mode: getCalendar/import errors in the async reschedule loop are not handled gracefully and can surface as unhandled rejections. The candidate is more specific about forEach not awaiting and proposes Promise.all with per-item catch, which aligns with the golden suggestion to catch around the await.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
async forEach callback makes the surrounding try/catch dead and leaves errors unhandled

This has the same problem as vital/lib/reschedule.ts. `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })` discards the promises it creates.

The enclosing `try/catch` (lines 124-139) therefore never catches anything. Errors from `getCalendar` or from the calendar/video deletion become unhandled rejections, which can crash the process. The deletions are also never awaited before the function returns.

Replace this with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try block.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify unawaited async forEach callbacks causing unhandled rejections and ineffective try/catch, and recommend awaiting Promise.all over mapped async callbacks.

false_positives.candidate:
getCalendar promise is created and dropped for non-"calendar" variants, risking unhandled rejection

In `getCalendarCredentials`, `getCalendar(credential)` is called for every credential of every `_calendar` app. That includes `*_other_calendar` CRM apps whose `variant` is not `"calendar"`, and for those the result is thrown away (`return app.variant === "calendar" ? [...] : []`).

`getCalendar` is now async, so a failure while constructing the service becomes a rejected promise that nobody awaits. Examples are `symmetricDecrypt` failing in the CloseCom/Salesforce services, or a schema parse error. That surfaces as an unhandled rejection instead of an error the caller can handle.

It also needlessly loads and instantiates services for credentials that are never used. Only call `getCalendar` when `app.variant === "calendar"`.

Recurring-cancel branch still uses forEach(async) so calendar deletions are never awaited

The non-credentialId branch was correctly converted to a `for...of` loop with `await getCalendar`. The recurring branch was only patched to `const calendar = await getCalendar(credential)` inside `.forEach(async (credential) => ...)`.

In that branch, `apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent)` runs only after the awaits. By then `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 has usually already run, and `sendCancelledEmails` and the response go out first. Deletion failures there are unhandled rejections.

The extra `await getCalendar` adds one more async hop before anything is recorded. Convert this to a `for...of` loop that pushes the `deleteEvent` promises, as was done for the sibling branch.
